stem: Which of the following represents the correct craniocaudal sequence of the five primitive cardiac sacculations before looping occurs?

choices.text: Sinus venosus → Atrium → Ventricle → Bulbus cordis → Truncus arteriosus
choices.rationale: This represents the reverse caudocranial direction.

choices.text: Truncus arteriosus → Bulbus cordis → Ventricle → Atrium → Sinus venosus
choices.rationale: The most cephalic dilatation is the truncus arteriosus, followed caudally by bulbus cordis, ventricle, atrium, and sinus venosus.

choices.text: Bulbus cordis → Truncus arteriosus → Ventricle → Atrium → Sinus venosus
choices.rationale: Truncus arteriosus is the most cephalic dilation, superior to bulbus cordis.

choices.text: Truncus arteriosus → Ventricle → Bulbus cordis → Sinus venosus → Atrium
choices.rationale: Bulbus cordis directly connects truncus arteriosus to the primitive ventricle.

explanation: The early embryonic heart tube develops five dilated sacculations in craniocaudal order: Truncus arteriosus (most cephalic), Bulbus cordis, Ventricle, Atrium, and Sinus venosus (most caudal bifurcation).
examTip: Truncus arteriosus gives rise to the roots of the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.

evidence.quote: The heart tube begins to show five sacculations. The most cephalic one is the truncus arteriosuswhich is followed by the bulbus cordis, ventricle, atrium and then the sinus venosus.

stem: During atrial partitioning, what embryological event maintains right-to-left shunting before the foramen primum is completely obliterated by the endocardial cushions?

choices.rationale: Ductus venosus is an intrahepatic vascular shunt, not involved in atrial septation.

choices.text: Formation of perforations in the upper part of septum primum that coalesce into the foramen secundum
choices.rationale: Multiple apoptotic perforations appear in the superior portion of the septum primum and coalesce to form the foramen secundum (ostium secundum).

choices.text: Downward growth of the thick muscular septum secundum
choices.rationale: Septum secundum forms later and forms the foramen ovale, not the foramen secundum.

choices.text: Absorption of the left horn of sinus venosus into the left atrium
choices.rationale: Left horn forms the coronary sinus and connects to the right atrium.

explanation: Before the foramen primum completely closes at the AV cushions, apoptosis produces multiple fenestrations in the superior region of the septum primum. These coalesce to form the foramen secundum, ensuring uninterrupted interatrial blood flow from right to left.
examTip: Excessive resorption of septum primum or defective septum secundum growth leads to an Ostium Secundum ASD (the most common type of ASD).

evidence.quote: allows free communication between the 2 atria. Thus the foramen primum is bounded above by the lower crescentric margin of the septum primum and below by a growing sub-endocardial cushion

stem: Which congenital heart anomaly represents the most common cause of cyanotic heart disease presenting in newborn infants in the first days of life?

choices.rationale: VSD is the most common congenital heart anomaly overall, but causes an acyanotic (left-to-right) shunt initially.
TGA is the most common cause of cyanotic congenital heart disease in neonates due to failure of spiral twisting of the aorticopulmonary septum.
PDA causes an acyanotic left-to-right shunt from aorta to pulmonary artery.
Coarctation causes blood pressure discrepancies and left ventricular overload without primary cyanosis.

explanation: Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA) occurs when the conotruncal (aorticopulmonary) septum fails to follow its normal 180-degree spiral course, resulting in the aorta arising from the RV and the pulmonary trunk from the LV. It is the most common cause of neonatal cyanotic heart disease.
examTip: TGA creates two parallel, non-communicating circuits. Survival depends on an intercirculatory shunt (PDA, ASD, or VSD).

evidence.quote: TGA is the most common cause of cyanotic heart disease in newborn infants.

stem: In the developing vascular system, what adult arterial structure is derived from the left fourth aortic arch?

choices.rationale: Third aortic arches give rise to the common carotid and proximal internal carotid arteries.

choices.text: A portion of the definitive Arch of the Aorta
choices.rationale: The left fourth aortic arch forms the segment of the arch of the aorta between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.
Ductus arteriosus is derived from the distal part of the left sixth (pulmonary) aortic arch.
The first aortic arch leaves behind the maxillary artery.

explanation: Aortic arch derivatives: 1st forms maxillary; 2nd forms stapedial and hyoid; 3rd forms common carotid and proximal internal carotid; left 4th forms part of the arch of aorta; right 4th forms proximal right subclavian; 5th disappears completely; left 6th forms left pulmonary artery and ductus arteriosus.
examTip: Remember: 4th arch = 4 limbs of Aorta on the left, right subclavian on the right. 6th arch = pulmonary arch.

evidence.quote: Left dorsal aorta -Distal part of aortic arch. Caudal to the pharyngeal arches the dorsal aortae fuse to form single descending aorta.

stem: Following birth and first respiration, what fibrous ligamentous cord represents the obliterated remnant of the left umbilical vein?

choices.rationale: Ligamentum arteriosum is the obliterated remnant of the ductus arteriosus (6th arch).
Ligamentum venosum is the remnant of the ductus venosus.

choices.text: Ligamentum teres hepatis (Round ligament of liver)
choices.rationale: The left umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from placenta to liver, closes after birth to form the ligamentum teres hepatis in the falciform ligament.
Medial umbilical ligaments are remnants of the distal umbilical arteries.

explanation: In the fetus, the left umbilical vein carries highly oxygenated blood from the placenta to the ductus venosus and IVC. After birth, thrombosis and fibrous obliteration convert it into the ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver).
examTip: Ductus venosus → Ligamentum venosum. Umbilical vein → Ligamentum teres hepatis. Umbilical arteries → Medial umbilical ligaments.

evidence.quote: Fate of umbilical veins: Left umbilical carries oxygenated blood, obliterates after birth to form ligamentum teres hepatis.

stem: Which coronary vessel supplies the posterior third of the interventricular septum and determines cardiac dominance in approximately 85% to 90% of individuals?

choices.rationale: LAD supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum.

choices.text: Posterior interventricular artery arising from the Right Coronary Artery
choices.rationale: In right-dominant hearts (~85-90%), the posterior descending artery (PDA) arises from the right coronary artery to supply the posterior 1/3 of the septum.

choices.text: Circumflex branch of Left Coronary Artery
choices.rationale: Circumflex gives off the PDA only in left-dominant hearts (~10%).
Marginal branch supplies the inferior and lateral wall of the right ventricle.

explanation: Cardiac dominance is defined by which coronary artery gives origin to the posterior interventricular artery (posterior descending artery, PDA). In ~85-90% of cases, the PDA arises from the right coronary artery (right dominance) and supplies the posterior 1/3 of the IV septum and AV node.
examTip: LAD supplies anterior 2/3 of IV septum + apex. PDA supplies posterior 1/3 of IV septum. Occlusion of RCA can cause AV block.

evidence.sourceName: 2nd year cvs anatomy of heart and mediastnum hanout.pdf
evidence.location: Page 23 - Blood supply of the heart
evidence.quote: Branches of the right coronary artery: posterior interventricular branch runs in the posterior interventricular groove to the apex.

stem: What is the innermost layer of the heart wall that lines the cardiac chambers and covers the valves?

choices.rationale: Epicardium is the outermost visceral layer of the serous pericardium.
Pericardium is the fibroserous sac surrounding the external surface of the heart.
Myocardium is the middle muscular layer responsible for contraction.
Endocardium is the innermost layer consisting of endothelium, smooth muscle/connective tissue, and subendocardial layer.

explanation: The heart wall has three layers: endocardium (innermost simple squamous endothelium and subendocardial connective tissue), myocardium (middle cardiac muscle), and epicardium (outer serous layer).
examTip: Purkinje conducting fibers are specifically located within the loose subendocardial connective tissue layer of the endocardium.

evidence.quote: The endocardium : Innermost layer of the heart (lines the atria and ventricles and covers the heart valves)

stem: Which valve guards the atrioventricular orifice between the left atrium and the left ventricle?

choices.rationale: The mitral (bicuspid) valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle.
The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular orifice.
The pulmonary valve guards the orifice of the pulmonary trunk from the right ventricle.
The aortic valve guards the vestibule of the left ventricle opening into the ascending aorta.

explanation: Cardiac valves are endocardial folds supported by internal plates of dense collagenous and elastic connective tissue continuous with the cardiac skeleton. The left atrioventricular valve is the mitral (bicuspid) valve.
examTip: In rheumatic heart disease, the mitral valve is the most frequently damaged valve (Mitral > Aortic > Tricuspid).

evidence.quote: What is the name of the valve between the left atrium and left ventricle? Mitral valve.

stem: In which anatomical layer of the cardiac wall are the impulse-conducting Purkinje fibers situated?

choices.rationale: Purkinje fibers reside in the subendocardial connective tissue layer of the endocardium.
Contractile working myocytes make up the myocardium, while specialized conducting Purkinje fibers travel in the subendocardium.
Epicardium contains adipose tissue and coronary vessels, not Purkinje fibers.
Fibrous pericardium is external connective tissue.

explanation: Purkinje fibers are modified cardiac muscle cells specialized for electrical conduction. They are larger than ordinary cardiac myocytes, stain paler due to abundant glycogen and mitochondria with fewer peripheral myofibrils, and travel in the subendocardial layer.
examTip: Histologically, Purkinje cells have abundant glycogen and mitochondria and fewer peripheral myofibrils compared to working myocytes.

evidence.quote: Purkinje fibers are located in which of the heart layer? Endocardium.

stem: Under microscopic examination, how does the wall of a large artery differ most prominently from that of a companion vein of similar diameter?

choices.text: The tunica adventitia is the thickest coat in the artery
choices.rationale: Tunica adventitia is the thickest layer in veins, not arteries.

choices.text: The tunica media is the thickest coat in the artery and contains prominent elastic laminae
choices.rationale: In arteries, the tunica media is by far the thickest tunic, packed with circular smooth muscle and wavy elastic membranes.

choices.text: Arteries lack an internal elastic lamina
choices.rationale: Internal elastic lamina is prominent in arteries and absent or rudimentary in veins.

choices.text: Arteries have a wider, collapsible irregular lumen
choices.rationale: Veins have large collapsible lumens; arteries have round, patent lumens.

explanation: Walls of both arteries and veins possess three tunics (intima, media, adventitia). In arteries, the tunica media is the thickest layer, allowing them to withstand and dampen systolic pressures. In veins, the tunica adventitia is the thickest coat.
examTip: Tunica media = thickest in arteries. Tunica adventitia = thickest in veins.

evidence.quote: Under the microscope, the tunica media is the thickest layer in arteries, and is much thicker in arteries than it is in veins.

stem: Which type of blood capillary is characterized by a discontinuous basement membrane, wide intercellular gaps between endothelial cells, and is specifically found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow?

choices.rationale: Continuous capillaries have unbroken basement membranes and tight junctions (e.g. muscle, lungs, CNS).
Fenestrated capillaries have pores (60-80 nm) with a continuous basement membrane (endocrine glands, renal glomeruli).
Sinusoidal capillaries possess wide intercellular gaps and incomplete or absent basement membranes to permit whole-cell passage.
Metarterioles are precapillary resistance vessels with discontinuous smooth muscle precapillary sphincters.

explanation: Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries have large irregular lumens, wide open fenestrae without diaphragms, and an incomplete or absent basement membrane. They are adapted for maximum exchange of macromolecules and cells in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.
examTip: Continuous = tight junctions + intact basal lamina (Blood-Brain Barrier). Fenestrated = pores + intact basal lamina (kidney). Sinusoid = open gaps + broken basal lamina (liver, spleen).

evidence.quote: Sinusoidal capillaries, or sinusoids, can be found in the liver, spleen and bone marrow. Endothelial cells have large openings and incomplete basement membrane.

stem: What is the primary physiological function and innervation of the Carotid Body located at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery?

choices.text: Baroreceptor sensing arterial blood pressure changes, innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve
choices.rationale: The Carotid Sinus (dilated wall of internal carotid) is the baroreceptor, not the carotid body.

choices.text: Chemoreceptor sensing changes in blood O2, CO2, and pH, innervated by CN IX and CN X
choices.rationale: The carotid body contains glomus cells that function as peripheral chemoreceptors responding to hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis.

choices.text: Thermoreceptor sensing core temperature, innervated by sympathetic fibers
choices.rationale: Carotid body does not function as a thermoreceptor.

choices.text: Endocrine gland secreting atrial natriuretic peptide into the systemic circulation
choices.rationale: ANP is secreted by atrial myocytes, not the carotid body.

explanation: The Carotid Sinus is a baroreceptor (mechanoreceptor monitoring arterial blood pressure in the dilated wall of the internal carotid). In contrast, the Carotid Body is a chemoreceptor monitoring arterial pO2, pCO2, and pH, innervated predominantly by the sinus nerve of CN IX and branches of CN X.
examTip: Carotid Sinus = Baroreceptor (Pressure). Carotid Body = Chemoreceptor (Blood gases/chemistry).

evidence.quote: 2- Carotid Body: Functions as a chemoreceptor, sensitive to low oxygen, high carbon dioxide, and low pH.

stem: A 10-year-old boy develops migratory polyarthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 3 weeks after an untreated pharyngitis. What is the fundamental immunological mechanism causing this cardiac injury?

choices.text: Direct persistent bacterial invasion of heart valves by Streptococcus pyogenes
choices.rationale: Rheumatic fever is a sterile, non-suppurative post-streptococcal complication, not active bacteremia.

choices.text: Molecular mimicry where anti-M protein antibodies cross-react with cardiac myosin (Type II hypersensitivity)
choices.rationale: Antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin via molecular mimicry, provoking a Type II hypersensitivity autoimmune reaction.

choices.text: Deposition of circulating antigen-antibody complexes in endocardium (Type III hypersensitivity)
choices.rationale: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is Type III; rheumatic fever is Type II hypersensitivity.
Streptococcal toxic shock is superantigen-mediated; rheumatic fever is antibody cross-reactivity.

explanation: Rheumatic fever results from molecular mimicry: antibodies formed against the M protein of Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes cross-react with normal human cardiac myosin, leading to a Type II hypersensitivity inflammatory reaction (pancarditis).
examTip: Remember: Acute rheumatic fever follows streptococcal PHARYNGITIS, never streptococcal skin infections (impetigo/erysipelas).
mnemonic: JONES Criteria: Joints, ♥ (Pancarditis), Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea

evidence.quote: antibodies formed against M protein of Group A β-hemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) (GAS) may cross react with the heart tissues (myosin) and cause rheumatic fever→ type II hypersensitivity reaction

stem: Which of the following clinical presentations of Streptococcus pyogenes infection is NOT associated with the subsequent development of acute rheumatic fever?

choices.rationale: Strep throat is the classic antecedent infection for rheumatic fever.
Strep tonsillitis is an upper respiratory GAS infection capable of triggering rheumatic fever.
Rheumatic fever is strictly NOT associated with streptococcal skin infections (e.g. impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis).

choices.text: Severe Group A streptococcal sore throat without antibiotic therapy
choices.rationale: Untreated pharyngeal strep carries the highest risk of ARF.

explanation: According to the faculty microbiology handout, rheumatic fever is a sequela of GAS upper respiratory tract infections (pharyngitis/tonsillitis). It is explicitly NOT associated with streptococcal skin infections such as impetigo or erysipelas (which can cause glomerulonephritis, but not rheumatic fever).
examTip: Strep skin infection (impetigo) → Post-streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) ONLY. Pharyngitis → Both ARF and PSGN.

evidence.quote: Rheumatic fever is not associated with streptococcal skin infections (e.g.,erysipelas, impetigo, cellulitis).

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of congenital bicuspid aortic valve undergoes dental extraction without antibiotic prophylaxis. Two months later, he presents with low-grade fever, malaise, and a new cardiac murmur. What is the most likely causative pathogen?

choices.rationale: S. aureus causes acute endocarditis on normal valves with rapid destruction, often in IV drug users.

choices.text: Viridans group Streptococci (e.g., S. sanguinis, S. mutans)
choices.rationale: Viridans streptococci are normal oral flora that cause subacute bacterial endocarditis on previously damaged or abnormal valves following dental work.
Pseudomonas is associated with prosthetic valves or IV drug users, presenting acutely.
Coxsackie B is a principal cause of viral myocarditis/pericarditis, not bacterial endocarditis.

explanation: Viridans group streptococci (Streptococcus sanguinis, S. mutans, S. mitis) are normal inhabitants of the oropharynx. Transient bacteremia following dental procedures allows these low-virulence organisms to adhere to pre-existing endothelial damage on abnormal valves via dextran production, producing subacute infective endocarditis.
examTip: Dental procedure + abnormal valve = Viridans streptococci (Subacute). IV drug user + normal tricuspid valve = Staphylococcus aureus (Acute).

evidence.quote: Viridans streptococci (50-60% of cases of subacute endocarditis): part of normal oral flora, usually affect abnormal or damaged valves following dental procedures.

stem: Which infectious agent is recognized as the most common viral cause of acute infectious myocarditis and pericarditis in young adults?

choices.rationale: Coxsackievirus group B is the most frequent viral pathogen causing acute inflammatory myocarditis in children and young adults.
HCV primarily infects hepatocytes and is not a primary cause of acute myocarditis.
Rotavirus is an enteric pathogen causing pediatric diarrhea, not myocarditis.
EBV causes infectious mononucleosis; cardiac involvement is very rare.

explanation: Coxsackievirus B (a single-stranded positive-sense RNA enterovirus of the Picornaviridae family) is the primary viral cause of myocarditis. It binds to the CAR (coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor) on cardiac myocytes, causing direct cytotoxic myocyte necrosis followed by secondary immune-mediated lymphocytic infiltration.
examTip: Young adult with flu-like illness followed by sudden chest pain, dyspnea, elevated troponin, and ST-segment changes without coronary blockage = Coxsackie B Myocarditis.

evidence.quote: Etiology: Coxsackieviruses group B are the most common cause of viral myocarditis.

stem: During cardiac bypass surgery, a surgeon passes a finger through the transverse pericardial sinus to clamp the great arterial trunks. Which anatomical structures lie directly ANTERIOR to the surgeon's finger?

choices.text: Superior vena cava and right atrium
choices.rationale: The superior vena cava and left atrium lie posterior to the transverse pericardial sinus.
The transverse pericardial sinus lies behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, and in front of the superior vena cava and atria.

choices.text: Inferior vena cava and left ventricle
choices.rationale: The inferior vena cava is situated inferiorly and related to the oblique pericardial sinus.
The pulmonary veins bound the oblique pericardial sinus posteriorly.

explanation: The transverse pericardial sinus is a passage between the arterial and venous ends of the heart tube. It is bounded anteriorly by the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, and posteriorly by the superior vena cava, right atrium, and left atrium.
examTip: A clamp passed through the transverse sinus controls hemorrhage from both the aorta and pulmonary trunk simultaneously.

evidence.sourceName: 2nd year cvs anatomy of heart and mediastnum hanout.pdf
evidence.quote: Pericardial sinuses : There are two sinuses between the parietal and visceral layers of the pericardium, the transverse sinus and the oblique sinus of the pericardium.

stem: A blind recess of the serous pericardial cavity situated behind the base of the heart (left atrium) is bounded laterally by the pulmonary veins and inferior vena cava. Which pericardial space is this?

choices.rationale: The transverse sinus is an open channel connecting both sides, lying between the great arteries and veins.
The oblique pericardial sinus is a cul-de-sac behind the left atrium, bounded by the reflections around the pulmonary veins and IVC.
This is a pleural recess between the costal and diaphragmatic pleurae.
Sulcus on the heart surface, not an intrapericardial serous sinus.

explanation: The oblique pericardial sinus is a wide, pocket-like recess behind the left atrium. It is bounded anteriorly by the back of the left atrium and posteriorly by the parietal pericardium overlying the esophagus and thoracic aorta.
examTip: The hand can enter the oblique sinus from below until it meets the reflection of serous pericardium forming a blind cul-de-sac.

evidence.sourceName: 2nd year cvs anatomy of heart and mediastnum hanout.pdf
evidence.quote: There are two sinuses between the parietal and visceral layers of the pericardium, the transverse sinus and the oblique sinus of the pericardium.

stem: A 28-year-old man with acute pericarditis complains of sharp retrosternal chest pain that radiates directly to the tip of his left shoulder. Which nerve carries the somatic sensory fibers responsible for this referred pain?

choices.rationale: The vagus nerve carries parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to the cardiac plexus.
The fibrous pericardium and parietal layer of serous pericardium are innervated by somatic sensory fibers of the phrenic nerves (C3, C4, C5), referring pain to the supraclavicular shoulder region.
The intercostobrachial nerve supplies the axilla and inner arm, mediating angina pectoris referral, not somatic pericardial pain.
Splanchnic nerves supply foregut abdominal viscera.

explanation: The fibrous and parietal pericardium receive somatic sensory innervation from the phrenic nerves (roots C3, C4, C5). Because the supraclavicular nerves supplying the skin of the shoulder share the same spinal cord segments (C3-C4), pericardial inflammation produces referred shoulder tip pain.
examTip: Pericardial pain is sharp, pleuritic, changes with posture (relieved by sitting forward), and radiates to the trapezius ridge (phrenic nerve).
mnemonic: C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm (and pericardium!) alive

evidence.sourceName: 2nd year cvs anatomy of heart and mediastnum hanout.pdf
evidence.quote: The pericardium is a sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels. It lies within the middle mediastinum.

stem: Which internal landmark inside the right atrium demarcates the boundary between the smooth-walled sinus venarum posteriorly and the trabeculated musculi pectinati anteriorly?

choices.rationale: The fossa ovalis is located on the interatrial septum, representing the obliterated foramen ovale.
The crista terminalis is a vertical muscular crest that separates the smooth-walled sinus venarum from the trabeculated pectinate muscle area.
The tendon of Todaro forms a boundary of Koch's triangle, not the main division of the RA cavity.
Guards the coronary sinus opening (Thebesian valve).

explanation: The crista terminalis is a prominent internal vertical muscular ridge extending from the anterior margin of the SVC opening to the IVC opening. Externally, it corresponds to the sulcus terminalis.
examTip: The SA node is situated at the upper end of the crista terminalis near the SVC orifice.

evidence.quote: This crista terminalis is the mark which diffeniate the sinal part from that of the atrial part. The sinal part is smooth and lies behind the crista terminalis while the atrial part is rough and found infront of the crista terminalis.

stem: During right ventriculotomy, a prominent curved muscular bundle extending from the interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle is identified. What crucial structure does this band transmit?

choices.text: Left bundle branch of the conducting system
choices.rationale: The left bundle branch travels down the left side of the muscular IV septum into the left ventricle.

choices.text: Right bundle branch of the atrioventricular bundle
choices.rationale: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) conveys the right branch of the AV bundle (bundle of His) to the anterior papillary muscle and RV free wall.
The circumflex artery is a branch of the left coronary artery in the coronary sulcus.
The great cardiac vein runs in the anterior interventricular sulcus.

explanation: The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) is a specialized muscular band in the right ventricle connecting the lower part of the ventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle. It carries the right bundle branch, facilitating coordinated anterior papillary contraction prior to ventricular systole.
examTip: Damage to the moderator band during surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot or VSD can cause right bundle branch block (RBBB).

evidence.sourceName: 2nd year cvs anatomy of heart and mediastnum hanout.pdf
evidence.quote: The right branch passes down on the right side of the ventricular septum to reach the moderator band

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the normal anatomy of the left atrium is anatomically ACCURATE?

choices.text: Its internal wall is lined almost entirely by coarse musculi pectinati
choices.rationale: The main cavity of the left atrium is smooth; pectinati are confined strictly to its small auricle.

choices.text: It receives four pulmonary veins that lack anatomical valves
choices.rationale: Four pulmonary veins (two right, two left) open into the smooth posterior wall of the left atrium and have no valves.

choices.text: It forms the major part of the sternocostal surface of the heart
choices.rationale: The sternocostal surface is formed mainly by the right ventricle and partly by the right atrium.

choices.text: Its walls are thinner than those of the right atrium
choices.rationale: The left atrium has thicker walls than the right atrium to overcome the high resistance of the thick LV wall.

explanation: The left atrium forms the major part of the base (posterior surface) of the heart. It receives four pulmonary veins without valves. Its internal lining is predominantly smooth, derived from incorporation of the embryonic pulmonary veins, with musculi pectinati restricted to the left auricle.
examTip: The left atrium lies directly anterior to the esophagus; left atrial enlargement (e.g. in mitral stenosis) can compress the esophagus and cause dysphagia.

evidence.sourceName: 2nd year cvs anatomy of heart and mediastnum hanout.pdf
evidence.quote: This chamber has slightly thicker walls than the right atrium because increased effort is required during atrial systole to overcome the elasticity of the extremely thick left ventricular wall. The left atrium consists of a main cavity and an auricle. The interior of the left atrium is smooth but its auricle has few and small musculi pectinati

stem: What is the primary physiological function of the central fibrous skeleton of the heart in addition to providing mechanical support for the four cardiac valves?

choices.text: Facilitating rapid electrical transmission between atria and ventricles across the AV groove
choices.rationale: It blocks direct conduction, acting as an electrical insulator.

choices.text: Acting as an electrical insulator that forces impulses to pass exclusively through the AV bundle
choices.rationale: The dense fibrous tissue provides electrical insulation, preventing random conduction between atrial and ventricular myocardium so impulses only pass via the AV bundle.

choices.text: Secreting atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) during atrial distension
choices.rationale: ANP is synthesized and secreted by atrial cardiomyocytes, not fibrous skeleton connective tissue.

choices.text: Providing collateral blood supply to the subendocardial conduction fibers
choices.rationale: The fibrous skeleton is avascular dense connective tissue.

explanation: The fibrous skeleton consists of four dense collagenous rings and two trigones (right and left fibrous trigones). It anchors the valve cusps, prevents valvular distension during systole, and electrically isolates the atria from the ventricles, ensuring that the atrioventricular (AV) bundle of His is the sole electrical conduit.
examTip: Accessory pathways (e.g. bundle of Kent in WPW syndrome) represent abnormal muscular bridges that bypass the insulating fibrous skeleton.

evidence.quote: This skeleton provides structure and support for the heart, as well as isolating the atria from the ventricles.

stem: From which aortic sinuses of Valsalva do the right and left coronary arteries normally arise?

choices.text: Right coronary from anterior aortic sinus; left coronary from left posterior aortic sinus
choices.rationale: The right coronary artery arises from the anterior (right) aortic sinus, and the left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus. The right posterior sinus is the non-coronary sinus.

choices.text: Right coronary from right posterior sinus; left coronary from left posterior sinus
choices.rationale: Right posterior sinus is non-coronary; RCA arises from the anterior sinus.

choices.text: Both coronaries arise from the anterior aortic sinus
choices.rationale: The left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus.

choices.text: Both coronaries arise from the pulmonary trunk sinuses
choices.rationale: Origin of coronaries from the pulmonary trunk is an abnormal anomaly (ALCAPA).

explanation: The aortic valve has three sinuses: one anterior and two posterior (left and right). The right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus, and the left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus. The right posterior aortic sinus gives rise to no coronary artery and is thus called the non-coronary sinus.
examTip: Coronary perfusion occurs predominantly during ventricular diastole when aortic recoil fills the sinuses of Valsalva.

evidence.sourceName: 2nd year cvs anatomy of heart and mediastnum hanout.pdf
evidence.quote: In healthy young individuals, most of the arteries are true end-arteries, which supply discrete volumes of the myocardium.

concept: Cardiac Venous Drainage and Coronary Sinus
stem: Which cardiac vein ascends in the posterior interventricular sulcus alongside the posterior descending artery (PDA) before terminating into the coronary sinus?

choices.rationale: Accompanies the anterior interventricular artery (LAD).
The middle cardiac vein (posterior interventricular vein) ascends in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior descending artery.
Runs in the coronary sulcus with the marginal branch of the RCA.
Cross the coronary sulcus to drain directly into the right atrium.

explanation: The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove with the posterior interventricular branch of the RCA (or LCx) and empties directly into the right end of the coronary sinus.
examTip: Great vein = anterior (with LAD); Middle vein = posterior (with PDA); Small vein = with acute marginal.

evidence.quote: The coronary sinus extends along the back of the atrio- ventricular groove to open into the right atrium just on the left of the inferior vena caval opening.

stem: Where is the sinoatrial (SA) node anatomically situated in the human heart?

choices.text: At the junction of the superior vena cava and the upper border of the crista terminalis in the right atrium
choices.rationale: The SA node lies subepicardially in the anterolateral wall of the right atrium at the upper end of the crista terminalis, just inferior to the opening of the SVC.

stem: Why is the muscular myocardium of the left ventricle approximately three times thicker than that of the right ventricle in the normal adult heart?

choices.text: Because the left ventricle must generate sufficient pressure to overcome systemic vascular resistance (~120 mmHg vs ~25 mmHg)
choices.rationale: The left ventricle pumps against the high-resistance systemic circulation (mean arterial pressure ~90-100 mmHg; peak systolic ~120 mmHg), whereas the right ventricle pumps into the low-resistance pulmonary circuit (~25/10 mmHg).

choices.text: Because the left ventricle holds twice the stroke volume of the right ventricle
choices.rationale: In the steady state, both ventricles must pump the exact same stroke volume (~70 mL) to prevent pulmonary congestion.

choices.text: Because the left ventricle receives twice the coronary perfusion flow during systole
choices.rationale: Left ventricular coronary perfusion occurs almost entirely during diastole due to high intramyocardial systolic pressure compressing the vessels.

choices.text: Because the left ventricle lacks papillary muscles and chordae tendineae
choices.rationale: The left ventricle possesses two large papillary muscles (anterior and posterior).

explanation: The adult left ventricle has a wall thickness of 8-12 mm, compared to 3-5 mm for the right ventricle. This single error creates: 1) infundibular pulmonary stenosis, 2) overriding aorta, 3) large ventricular septal defect (VSD), and 4) secondary right ventricular hypertrophy.
examTip: Remember PROVe for Fallot: Pulmonary stenosis, Right ventricular hypertrophy, Overriding aorta, VSD.
mnemonic: PROVe: Pulmonary stenosis, RVH, Overriding aorta, VSD

evidence.quote: Furtherly, the aortic and pulmonary tubes are twisted in a spiral fashion, so that the sulcus is locked  dorsally in the middle of the distance, and then to the right while the right sulcus is locked ventrally and then to the left in the upper part of the distance.

stem: In Transposition of the Great Arteries (TGA), the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk arises from the left ventricle. What embryological failure produces this anomaly?

choices.text: Failure of the aorticopulmonary septum to follow its normal 180-degree spiral course
choices.rationale: TGA occurs when the aorticopulmonary septum grows straight downward rather than spiraling 180 degrees, leaving the aorta connected to the anterior right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk to the posterior left ventricle.

choices.text: Failure of development of the muscular interventricular septum
choices.rationale: Causes a common ventricle (single ventricle).

choices.text: Premature closure of the foramen ovale in utero
choices.rationale: Causes left ventricular hypoplasia.

choices.text: Obliteration of the left 6th aortic arch
choices.rationale: Prevents ductus arteriosus formation.

explanation: Transposition of the Great Arteries occurs when the conotruncal septum fails to spiral and instead divides the truncus longitudinally in a straight line. As a result, deoxygenated systemic venous blood from the RV is pumped back into the aorta, and oxygenated blood from the LV is pumped into the lungs, creating two independent parallel circuits.
examTip: TGA is incompatible with life unless a mixing shunt (patent ductus arteriosus, VSD, or ASD) is present. Infusion of prostaglandin E1 maintains PDA patency.

evidence.quote: Furtherly, the aortic and pulmonary tubes are twisted in a spiral fashion, so that the sulcus is locked  dorsally in the middle of the distance, and then to the right while the right sulcus is locked ventrally and then to the left in the upper part of the distance.

stem: Which adult arteries are derived from the embryonic third pair of aortic arches?

choices.text: Common carotid arteries and proximal portion of internal carotid arteries
choices.rationale: The third aortic arch forms the common carotid artery and the proximal segment of the internal carotid artery bilaterally (the distal internal carotid develops from the dorsal aorta).
Derived from the 1st aortic arch.
Derived from the 2nd aortic arch.

choices.text: Arch of aorta and right subclavian artery
choices.rationale: Derived from the 4th aortic arches.

explanation: The 3rd aortic arches give rise to the common carotid arteries and proximal part of the internal carotid arteries on both sides. The external carotid arteries sprout as new arterial buds from the third arch.
examTip: Arch 1 = Maxillary; Arch 2 = Stapedial/hyoid; Arch 3 = Carotids (C is 3rd letter of alphabet); Arch 4 = Aortic arch & Subclavian; Arch 6 = Pulmonaries & Ductus arteriosus.
mnemonic: 1 is max, 2 is step (stapes), 3 is C (Carotid)

evidence.quote: Third aortic arches: Form carotid arteries.

stem: What is the embryological fate of the left sixth aortic arch in human vascular development?

choices.text: Disappears completely without leaving any remnant
choices.rationale: The 5th arch disappears completely; the left 6th arch persists.

choices.text: Gives rise to the proximal left pulmonary artery and ductus arteriosus
choices.rationale: The left 6th aortic arch forms the proximal part of the left pulmonary artery and maintains communication with the dorsal aorta as the ductus arteriosus.

choices.text: Forms the distal portion of the right subclavian artery
choices.rationale: Derived from the right dorsal aorta.
Derived from the anterior cardinal vein anastomosis.

explanation: The 6th aortic arch (pulmonary arch) develops branches toward the lung buds. On the right, the distal part degenerates and the proximal part forms the proximal right pulmonary artery. On the left, the proximal part forms the proximal left pulmonary artery, and the distal part persists as the ductus arteriosus.
examTip: The persistence of the left 6th arch explains why the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around the ligamentum arteriosum in the thorax.

evidence.quote: Sixth aortic arches: Left 6th aortic arch Gives left pulmonary artery and ductus arteriosus.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is found to have hypertension in both arms (160/90 mmHg) with weak, delayed femoral pulses and bilateral inferior rib notching on chest radiograph. Which type of aortic coarctation is characteristically associated with this clinical presentation?

choices.text: Postductal (adult type) coarctation with constriction distal to the ductus arteriosus
choices.rationale: Adult type (postductal) coarctation involves narrowing distal to the ductus/ligamentum arteriosum. Collateral blood flow develops through dilated intercostal arteries, producing characteristic rib notching.

choices.text: Preductal (infant type) coarctation with persistent widely patent ductus arteriosus
choices.rationale: Preductal coarctation manifests in infancy with severe lower extremity cyanosis and ductal dependence without extensive collaterals or rib notching.

choices.text: Abdominal aortic coarctation at the renal arteries
choices.rationale: Does not cause rib notching of the thoracic rib cage.
Anatomical variation of aortic arch, not classic postductal rib-notching coarctation.

explanation: Adult (postductal) coarctation of the aorta occurs distal to the ligamentum arteriosum. Because the constriction develops gradually, extensive collaterals develop between the subclavian/internal thoracic arteries and descending aorta via posterior intercostal arteries. The pulsatile pressure erosion from these enlarged intercostals notches the underside of ribs 3-8.
examTip: Classic triad of adult coarctation: upper extremity hypertension, weak/delayed femoral pulses (radiofemoral delay), and inferior rib notching (Roesler's sign).

evidence.quote: Postductal (adult type): is more common type. DA is usually closed. The constriction is distal to DA. This permits development of collateral circulation between intercostal arteries, internal thoracic arteries and descending thoracic aorta

stem: Which embryonic venous structures fuse to form the superior vena cava (SVC)?

choices.text: Right anterior cardinal vein and right common cardinal vein
choices.rationale: The superior vena cava develops from the caudal portion of the right anterior cardinal vein and the entirety of the right common cardinal vein (duct of Cuvier).
Vitelline veins form the portal vein, hepatic veins, and hepatic segment of IVC.

choices.text: Right umbilical vein and ductus venosus
choices.rationale: Umbilical veins connect to the liver, not the SVC.

choices.text: Right subcardinal and right supracardinal veins
choices.rationale: Contribute to the inferior vena cava segments.

explanation: The superior vena cava forms from the caudal part of the right anterior cardinal vein and the right common cardinal vein. An oblique transverse shunt connecting the left and right anterior cardinal veins becomes the left brachiocephalic vein.
examTip: Persistence of the left anterior cardinal vein results in a persistent left superior vena cava, which typically drains into the coronary sinus.

evidence.quote: The Superior vena cava forms from the right anterior cardinal vein and the right common cardinal vein.

stem: From which embryonic venous vessel does the HEPATIC segment of the inferior vena cava derive?

choices.text: Cranial part of the right vitelline vein
choices.rationale: The hepatic segment of the IVC is derived from the proximal/cranial portion of the right vitelline vein (hepatocardiac channel).
Forms the oblique vein of the left atrium and coronary sinus.
Forms the renal segment of the IVC.
Forms the post-renal/sacrocardinal segment of the IVC.

explanation: The definitive IVC is a composite vessel assembled from four embryonic segments: 1) Hepatic segment (proximal right vitelline vein), 2) Prerenal segment (right subcardinal vein), 3) Renal segment (subcardinal-supracardinal anastomosis), and 4) Postrenal segment (right supracardinal/sacrocardinal vein).
examTip: Failure of the right subcardinal vein to connect with the hepatic segment results in 'absence of the hepatic segment of IVC' with azygos continuation.

evidence.quote: Development of inferior vena cava (IVC): -Hepatic segment from cranial part of right vitelline vein. -Renal segment from the right subcardinal vein. -Sacrocardinal segment from the right sacrocardinal vein.

stem: What is the primary physiological function of the ductus venosus in fetal circulation?

choices.text: To divert highly oxygenated umbilical venous blood directly into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic sinusoidal network
choices.rationale: The ductus venosus connects the umbilical vein to the IVC, allowing ~50% of oxygen-rich placental blood to bypass the high-resistance liver capillary bed and reach the heart rapidly.

choices.text: To return deoxygenated blood from the internal iliac arteries back to the placenta
choices.rationale: This is the function of the umbilical arteries.

choices.text: To shunt blood from the right ventricle into the descending aorta
choices.rationale: This is the function of the ductus arteriosus.

choices.text: To prevent mixing of coronary venous blood with systemic venous return
choices.rationale: Coronary venous blood drains via the coronary sinus.

explanation: Oxygenated blood (80% saturated) from the placenta travels up the umbilical vein. About half bypasses the liver sinusoids via the ductus venosus to enter the IVC directly. A muscular sphincter near its origin regulates flow; increased flow during uterine contractions prevents cardiac overload.
examTip: Postnatally, the ductus venosus obliterates within days and forms the fibrous ligamentum venosum in the liver fissure.

evidence.quote: The left branch of the portal vein also communicates with the inferior vena cava(I.V.C.) within the liver by a communicating duct, termed the ductus venosus.

stem: In which fetal blood vessel is the oxygen saturation of hemoglobin at its HIGHEST level in utero?

choices.rationale: The umbilical vein carries newly oxygenated blood directly from the placenta into the fetal body, boasting the highest oxygen saturation (~80%) of any vessel in the fetus.
Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated fetal blood back to the placenta (~58% saturation).
Contains mixed blood after receiving desaturated blood from the ductus arteriosus (~60%).
Carries desaturated venous blood returning from the upper body (~40%).

explanation: The umbilical vein brings freshly oxygenated, nutrient-rich maternal blood from the chorionic villi to the fetus with an SaO2 of approximately 80%. After mixing in the IVC with systemic venous return, the SaO2 falls to ~70%.
examTip: Order of oxygenation in fetus: Umbilical vein > Ductus venosus > IVC > Left ventricle/ascending aorta > Pulmonary trunk > Umbilical arteries.

evidence.quote: The oxygenated blood is conveyed from the placenta by the umbilical vein.

concept: Postnatal Functional Closure of Foramen Ovale
stem: What physiological event immediately triggers the functional closure of the foramen ovale upon the newborn infant's first breath?

choices.text: Increased pulmonary venous return raising left atrial pressure above right atrial pressure
choices.rationale: Lung expansion drops pulmonary vascular resistance dramatically, flooding the left atrium with blood. The resulting rise in left atrial pressure presses the flexible valve of the foramen ovale (septum primum) firmly against the septum secundum.

choices.text: Sudden surge in maternal prostaglandin E2
choices.rationale: Prostaglandins drop after placenta removal, which helps close the ductus arteriosus, not foramen ovale.

choices.text: Contraction of the umbilical vein sphincter
choices.rationale: Umbilical clamping stops placental flow, dropping IVC/RA pressure, but left atrial pressure increase drives the closure.

choices.text: Direct muscular constriction of the annulus ovalis by vagal stimulation
choices.rationale: Closure is driven by hemodynamics, not neural constriction.

explanation: At birth, lung expansion causes pulmonary vascular resistance to drop by 80%. Massive pulmonary blood flow returns through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium. Left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure, pressing the flap-like septum primum against the rigid septum secundum, functionally sealing the interatrial communication.
examTip: Functional closure occurs within minutes of birth; anatomical fibrous adhesion takes several months.

evidence.quote: As the venous blood is, forced into the lungs and returned back as an arterial blood towards the left atrium, the pressure into this atrium will increase and hence closure of the foramen oval by pressing the movable, flap- like, septum primum on the septum secondum.

stem: A premature infant is diagnosed with a large patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) causing pulmonary volume overload. Which medication is administered to pharmacologically stimulate closure of the ductus arteriosus?

choices.rationale: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX), reducing prostaglandin E1/E2 synthesis and triggering muscular constriction and closure of the ductus arteriosus.
Prostaglandins keep the ductus arteriosus OPEN in ductal-dependent lesions.
Inotropic agent; does not close the ductus.
Anticoagulant; does not induce PDA closure.

explanation: In utero, patency of the ductus arteriosus is maintained by low oxygen tension and high levels of circulating prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) from the placenta. Postnatally, NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin or ibuprofen) inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, promoting ductal smooth muscle constriction and closure.
examTip: Remember: 'Come in and CLOSE the door' (Indomethacin closes PDA); 'PGE keeps it PatEnt' (Prostaglandin keeps it open).
mnemonic: Indomethacin = In to CLOSE; Prostaglandin = Keep it Patent

evidence.quote: Prostaglandin infusion is given in an attempt to reopen DA.

stem: At what gestational time point does the human embryonic heart begin its first coordinated myogenic contractions?

choices.text: During the 3rd week of development (approx. Day 21-22)
choices.rationale: The primitive heart tube begins regular myogenic contractions around day 21-22 (during the 3rd week), prior to neural innervation or specialized conduction system differentiation.

choices.text: At the beginning of the 8th week
choices.rationale: By week 8, organogenesis is already complete.
Fetal heart movements can be detected by Doppler, but contractions start much earlier.
The heart does not form until gastrulation and cardiogenic tube fusion.

explanation: The cardiovascular system is the first organ system to become functional in the embryo. Peristaltic contractions begin during the 3rd week (day 22) as myocardial cells depolarize spontaneously.
examTip: Contractions precede functional valve formation and the histological differentiation of the SA/AV nodes.

evidence.quote: The hear starts to beat during the 3 rd week prior to development of the conducting system, and a circulation is established before a competent valvular mechanism.

stem: Following birth, the distal obliterated segments of the bilateral umbilical arteries persist on the anterior abdominal wall as which anatomical structures?

choices.rationale: The distal obliterated portions of the umbilical arteries form the fibrous cords known as the medial umbilical ligaments (producing the medial umbilical folds).
Formed by the obliterated urachus (allantois).
Raised by the inferior epigastric vessels.
Formed by the obliterated left umbilical vein.

explanation: The proximal parts of the umbilical arteries remain patent as the internal iliac and superior vesical arteries. The distal parts obliterate to form the fibrous medial umbilical ligaments on the posterior surface of the anterior abdominal wall.
examTip: MediaN = urachus (single, in midline); MediaL = paired umbilical arteries; Lateral = inferior epigastric arteries.
mnemonic: MediaN has an 'N' for Nine o'clock midline (urachus). MediaL has an 'L' for Leg arteries (umbilical).

evidence.quote: A condition which leads to obliteration and fibrosis of the distal parts of these arteries (down to the level of their superior vesical branches) forming the two medial umbilical ligaments.

stem: Which adult ligament represents the fibrous postnatal remnant of the left umbilical vein?

choices.text: Ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver)
choices.rationale: After birth, the left umbilical vein is obliterated and becomes the fibrous ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament), which runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament.
Postnatal remnant of the ductus venosus.
Postnatal remnant of the ductus arteriosus.
Peritoneal reflection enclosing the bare area of the liver.

explanation: The left umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. After birth and cord clamping, it thromboses and becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis in the lower free margin of the falciform ligament.
examTip: In severe portal hypertension, the umbilical vein remnant can recanalize (Cruveilhier-Baumgarten sign) causing caput medusae.

evidence.quote: resulting in its obliteration with the formation of the round ligament or ligamentum teres of the liver.

stem: A 34-year-old woman develops a sudden ischemic stroke following a deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in her right calf. Echocardiography with agitated saline bubble study reveals bubbles crossing from the right atrium to the left atrium during a Valsalva maneuver. What is the clinical term for this phenomenon?

choices.text: Paradoxical embolism across a patent foramen ovale (PFO)
choices.rationale: Transient elevation of right atrial pressure (e.g. during coughing or Valsalva) opens a probe-patent foramen ovale, permitting a venous embolus to pass from the right to left atrium and enter the systemic circulation (paradoxical embolus).
Clinical cyanotic crisis, not thromboembolic stroke.
Fixed irreversible pulmonary hypertension with shunt reversal from chronic VSD/ASD.
Microvascular redistribution of coronary flow away from stenosed vessels.

explanation: In ~25% of the normal population, the septum primum and septum secundum fail to completely fuse, leaving a potential probe-patent foramen ovale (PFO). While normally closed by left atrial pressure, maneuvers that raise intrathoracic and right atrial pressure (Valsalva, coughing) can reverse the pressure gradient and allow a deep venous thrombus to cross into the systemic arteries (paradoxical embolism).
examTip: PFO is the most common cause of cryptogenic stroke in young adults (<55 years old).

evidence.quote: The latter acts as a loose valvular flap which allows passage of blood from the right to the left but prevents the flow of blood in the reverse direction.

stem: An infant presents with stridor and difficulty swallowing (dysphagia). Barium swallow demonstrates bilateral extrinsic compression of the esophagus and trachea caused by a complete vascular ring surrounding both organs. What embryological anomaly produces this finding?

choices.text: Persistence of the distal portion of the right dorsal aorta forming a double aortic arch
choices.rationale: A double aortic arch results from the failure of the distal right dorsal aorta to regress, creating a vascular ring formed by right and left arches that encircle and compress the trachea and esophagus.

choices.text: Abnormal persistence of the right 6th aortic arch
choices.rationale: Does not form an encircling aortic vascular ring around the esophagus.

choices.text: Obliteration of the left 4th aortic arch
choices.rationale: Leads to interrupted aortic arch.

choices.text: Persistence of the left umbilical vein
choices.rationale: Does not affect the thoracic mediastinal vessels.

explanation: In normal development, the distal part of the right dorsal aorta regresses caudal to the 7th intersegmental artery. If it fails to involute, both right and left dorsal aortae persist, forming a complete arterial ring around the trachea and esophagus that produces stridor and dysphagia (dysphagia lusoria).
examTip: Double aortic arch is the most common symptomatic vascular ring anomaly causing tracheoesophageal compression in infants.

evidence.quote: 2-Double aortic arch: Mechanism is failure of distal part of right dorsal aorta to disappear.

concept: Ostium Secundum vs Ostium Primum ASD
stem: Which type of atrial septal defect (ASD) is caused by excessive resorption of the septum primum or inadequate development of the septum secundum?

choices.rationale: Ostium secundum ASD (accounting for ~90% of ASDs) is situated in the center of the interatrial septum at the fossa ovalis, caused by either excessive apoptosis of septum primum or incomplete growth of septum secundum.
Located low near the AV valves, caused by failure of endocardial cushion fusion.
Located near the entrance of the SVC, associated with anomalous pulmonary venous return.
Rare unroofed coronary sinus defect.

explanation: Ostium secundum defect is the most common type of atrial septal defect (90% of cases). It results from abnormal morphogenesis of the septum primum (excessive resorption forming huge fenestrations) or septum secundum (underdeveloped crescent that cannot cover foramen secundum).
examTip: Secundum ASD causes fixed wide splitting of S2 and a pulmonary flow murmur due to volume overload of the right heart.

evidence.quote: As the septum secondum grows downwards on the right of the remaining part of the septum primum, it does not form a complete partition. Thus, its lower concaved margin leaves an oval aperature  which is the foramen oval

concept: Left Horn of Sinus Venosus Fate
stem: What is the adult anatomical derivative of the left horn of the embryonic sinus venosus?

choices.text: Oblique vein of the left atrium (vein of Marshall) and coronary sinus
choices.rationale: As blood shifts to the right horn, the left horn of the sinus venosus regresses to form the oblique vein of the left atrium (vein of Marshall) and the coronary sinus.

choices.text: Smooth sinus venarum of the right atrium
choices.rationale: Derived from the right horn of sinus venosus.
Derived from the right venous valve.
Derived from the right anterior and common cardinal veins.

explanation: During the 5th to 7th weeks of development, the systemic venous return shifts toward the right side. The right horn of the sinus venosus enlarges to form the sinus venarum, while the left horn atrophies, leaving the oblique vein of the left atrium (vein of Marshall) and the coronary sinus.
examTip: The coronary sinus receives almost all cardiac venous return and empties into the right atrium between the IVC orifice and tricuspid valve.

evidence.quote: As the left horn becomes rudiment, it remains as the oblique vein of marshal which runs on the back of the left atrium. This vein opens into the coronary sinus which originates from the transverse coummunicating duct between the 2 horns.

stem: Which of the following adult venous structures is derived from the embryonic vitelline veins?

choices.text: Portal vein, hepatic sinusoids, and hepatic veins
choices.rationale: The vitelline veins form a complex anastomotic network around the duodenum that develops into the portal vein, liver sinusoids, hepatic veins, and the hepatic segment of the IVC.

choices.text: Superior vena cava and azygos vein
choices.rationale: Derived from anterior and common cardinal veins.
Derived from anterior cardinal veins.
Derived from the obliterated left umbilical vein.

explanation: The vitelline veins return blood from the yolk sac. As the liver cords invade them, they break into the hepatic sinusoids. The anastomotic plexus around the duodenum condenses to form the portal vein, and the cranial right vitelline vein forms the hepatic veins and hepatic IVC.
examTip: Vitelline veins = Portal system & hepatic sinusoids; Umbilical veins = Placental oxygenation (ligamentum teres); Cardinal veins = Caval system (SVC & IVC segments).

evidence.quote: Vitelline veins share in formation of: a)Liver sinusoids. b)Hepatic veins. c)Portal vein. d)Inferior vena cava.

stem: Which specialized intercellular junction in the longitudinal portion of the cardiac intercalated disc permits rapid ionic flow and synchronized electrical excitation between adjacent cardiomyocytes?

choices.rationale: Located in the transverse portion, serving as anchoring sites for actin filaments.
Gap junctions are clustered within the longitudinal component of the intercalated disc (parallel to myofibrils) to provide low-resistance ionic coupling for electrical syncytium.
Located in the transverse portion, providing mechanical tensile strength via desmin filaments.
Not a primary functional component of the cardiac intercalated disc.

explanation: Cardiac intercalated discs have two orientations: 1) Transverse portion (perpendicular to myofilaments at the Z line) contains fascia adherens (anchors actin) and desmosomes (binds desmin) for mechanical cohesion. 2) Longitudinal portion (parallel to myofilaments) contains extensive gap junctions that allow direct ion passage for rapid electrical conduction.
examTip: Transverse = mechanical anchor (fascia adherens + desmosomes); Longitudinal = electrical conduction (gap junctions).

evidence.quote: The longitudinal portion runs parallel to the myofilaments with many gap junctions to allow rapid spread of excitation between the adjacent cardio myocytes.

stem: Under light microscopy, how do subendocardial Purkinje conduction fibers differ cytologically from ordinary contractile ventricular cardiomyocytes?

choices.text: They are larger in diameter, have fewer peripheral myofibrils, and stain pale due to abundant sarcoplasmic glycogen
choices.rationale: Purkinje fibers are significantly larger/thicker than ordinary cardiomyocytes, contain fewer peripherally displaced myofibrils, have abundant mitochondria, and are rich in glycogen (producing pale H&E staining).

choices.text: They are smaller in diameter, densely packed with myofibrils, and lack glycogen reserves
choices.rationale: Ordinary contractile myocytes are narrower and packed with myofibrils.

choices.text: They possess multiple peripheral flattened nuclei identical to skeletal muscle fibers
choices.rationale: Purkinje fibers have 1-2 central, rounded nuclei.

choices.text: They lack intercalated discs and conduct impulses at the slowest velocity in the heart
choices.rationale: They contact myocytes via modified intercalated discs and conduct stimuli faster than any other cardiac tissue (2-4 m/s).

explanation: Purkinje fibers are specialized modified cardiac muscle cells found in the subendocardium. They are much larger and broader than working myocytes, rich in glycogen and mitochondria, have fewer sparse myofibrils located at the cell periphery, and often possess two central nuclei. Their structure is optimized for high-speed impulse propagation.
examTip: Purkinje cells wash out during standard histologic preparation due to high glycogen content, leaving pale 'ghost-like' cells.

evidence.quote: Modified cardiac muscle cells and  larger than  ordinary cardiac muscle with fewer myofibrils and many mitochondria . Compared to ordinary cardiac muscle cells: Contain large amounts of glycogen. Fewer myofibrils. * Thicker cells. Can be binucleated (cell contains 2 nuclei).

stem: What type of histological connective tissue forms the central structural framework of the cardiac skeleton (annuli fibrosi and fibrous trigones)?

choices.rationale: The cardiac skeleton is composed of dense white collagenous fibrous connective tissue, providing rigid mechanical anchorage and electrical isolation.
A common misconception tested in self-assessments; the skeleton is collagenous, NOT yellow elastic.
Areolar tissue lacks the tensile rigidity required to support valve annuli.
While cartilage-like in some large mammals (os cordis), in humans it is dense collagenous fibrous tissue.

explanation: The cardiac skeleton consists of dense irregular white collagenous connective tissue that surrounds the four cardiac orifices (annuli fibrosi) and fuses in the fibrous trigones. It anchors the valve cusps and prevents electrical conduction between atria and ventricles.
examTip: Self-assessment true/false trap: 'Cardiac skeleton is composed of dense yellow elastic tissue' -> FALSE! It is dense white fibrous/collagenous tissue.

evidence.quote: The central supporting structure of the heart is the "cardiac skeleton," composed of dense white fibrous (collagenous) connective tissue into which the cardiac muscle fibers of the atria and ventricles insert and to which the heart valves are attached.

stem: Which sublayer of the endocardium contains loose connective tissue, small blood vessels, and branches of the impulse-conducting Purkinje fibers?

choices.rationale: The subendocardial layer is the outermost layer of the endocardium that merges with the myocardium, containing loose connective tissue, nerves, and Purkinje fibers.
Innermost single layer of simple squamous cells.

choices.text: Middle smooth muscle and connective tissue layer
choices.rationale: Contains smooth muscle and elastic fibers, but Purkinje fibers reside in the subendocardial layer.
Located on the outer surface of the heart under the mesothelium.

explanation: The endocardium consists of three layers: 1) Endothelium (simple squamous cells resting on basal lamina), 2) Middle myoelastic layer (connective tissue and smooth muscle), and 3) Subendocardial layer (loose connective tissue housing the cardiac conduction system: Purkinje fibers).
examTip: Subendocardial ischemia occurs first in CAD because coronary perfusion pressure is lowest and wall stress is highest in this deepest layer.

evidence.quote: Sub endocardial Layer - outer layer of the endocardium is loose connective tissue joining the endocardium and myocardium. equivalent to tunica intima.

concept: Thickest Layer in Arteries vs Veins
stem: Comparing the three concentric wall layers under the microscope, which layer is characteristically the thickest in ARTERIES, and which is the thickest in VEINS?

choices.text: Arteries: Tunica media is thickest; Veins: Tunica adventitia is thickest
choices.rationale: Under the microscope, the tunica media is the thickest layer in arteries (to withstand high systolic pressures), whereas the tunica adventitia is normally the thickest layer in veins.

choices.text: Arteries: Tunica intima is thickest; Veins: Tunica media is thickest
choices.rationale: Tunica intima is thin in both, consisting of endothelium and subendothelium.

choices.text: Arteries: Tunica adventitia is thickest; Veins: Tunica intima is thickest
choices.rationale: Adventitia is thickest in veins, not arteries.

choices.text: Both arteries and veins have tunica media as their thickest layer
choices.rationale: The media of veins is thin with few muscle fibers; adventitia predominates in veins.

explanation: In arteries, the tunica media dominates to accommodate pressure and regulate peripheral resistance (muscular and elastic fibers). In veins, blood is under low pressure, so the tunica media is thin and underdeveloped; the tunica adventitia (connective tissue with collagen and longitudinal muscle) is the thickest coat.
examTip: Key histological contrast: Arteries = thick media, narrow lumen; Veins = thin media, thick adventitia, wide collapsed lumen.

evidence.quote: Under the microscope, the tunica media is the thickest layer in arteries, and is much thicker in arteries than it is in veins.

concept: Inferior Vena Cava Adventitial Smooth Muscle
stem: What unique histological specialization is present in the tunica adventitia of the INFERIOR VENA CAVA (IVC) to assist venous return toward the heart?

choices.text: Multiple fenestrated elastic lamellae alternating with chondrocytes
choices.rationale: Elastic lamellae are found in elastic arteries (aorta), not IVC.

choices.text: Longitudinally arranged bundles of smooth muscle fibers
choices.rationale: The tunica adventitia of the IVC contains prominent bundles of longitudinally oriented smooth muscle fibers whose peristaltic contraction propels blood upward against gravity.

choices.text: A thick, continuous internal elastic membrane
choices.rationale: Large veins lack an internal elastic lamina.

choices.text: Dense clusters of glomus chemoreceptor cells
choices.rationale: Glomus cells are found in the carotid body, not the IVC.

explanation: The inferior vena cava has a thin intima and media, but an exceptionally thick tunica adventitia containing longitudinally arranged fascicles of smooth muscle fibers. Contraction of these longitudinal smooth muscle bundles shortens the vessel and pumps venous blood against gravity toward the right atrium.
examTip: High-yield pathology/histology question: Longitudinal smooth muscle in the adventitia is diagnostic of large veins (especially IVC).

evidence.quote: NB. The inferior vena cava has longitudinally arranged bundles of smooth muscle fibers. Contraction of these muscle fibers helps in propelling blood towards the heart against gravity.

stem: In which tunic of large arteries and veins are the 'vasa vasorum' (vessels of vessels) primarily situated?

choices.text: Tunica adventitia (and outer portion of the tunica media)
choices.rationale: Vasa vasorum are located in the tunica adventitia and outer media of thick vessels to supply oxygen and nutrients to cells that cannot receive nourishment via simple diffusion from the luminal blood.

choices.text: Tunica intima directly beneath the endothelial basement membrane
choices.rationale: The intima is nourished directly by luminal diffusion.

choices.text: Deep within the internal elastic lamina
choices.rationale: The internal elastic lamina is an avascular acellular sheet of elastin.

choices.text: Exclusively in the endothelial cell cytoplasm
choices.rationale: Vasa vasorum are multicellular microvessels, not intracellular organelles.

explanation: Because the walls of large elastic arteries and great veins are thick (>29 cell layers), oxygen and nutrients cannot diffuse from the lumen to the outer layers. Vasa vasorum ('vessels of vessels') arborize within the tunica adventitia and outer media to nourish the vessel wall.
examTip: In syphilitic aortitis, endarteritis obliterans of the aortic adventitial vasa vasorum leads to ischemia of the aortic media, resulting in elastic tissue destruction and thoracic aortic aneurysms.

evidence.quote: Larger arteries and veins contain small blood vessels in the tunica adventitia known as the vasa vasorum to provide them with this vital exchange.

stem: Which contractile cells surround blood capillaries, are completely enclosed within the split basal lamina of endothelial cells, and can differentiate into smooth muscle or fibroblasts during tissue repair?

choices.rationale: Pericytes are branched, contractile mesenchymal cells nestled within the split basal lamina of capillaries and postcapillary venules that regulate microvascular flow and serve as progenitor cells.
Chemoreceptor cells of the carotid body.
Myelinating cells of the peripheral nervous system.
Granulocytic immune cells in connective tissue that release histamine.

explanation: Pericytes are perivascular contractile cells with long branching processes that wrap around capillaries. They reside inside the duplicated basal lamina of the endothelium. They modulate microvascular permeability, vessel tone, and possess pluripotency to differentiate into fibroblasts or smooth muscle cells following injury.
examTip: Loss of retinal pericytes is the earliest histological hallmark of diabetic retinopathy, causing microaneurysms and capillary leakage.

evidence.quote: The basal lamina split to enclose pericytes. Pericytes are flat branched contractile cells.

stem: What is the biological term for the bidirectional transport of macromolecules across the endothelial cell cytoplasm mediated by numerous pinocytotic vesicles?

choices.rationale: Transcytosis refers to vesicular transport where pinocytotic vesicles engulf macromolecules on one luminal surface and traverse the endothelial cytoplasm to exocytose on the opposite abluminal surface.
The transmigration of leukocytes across the vessel wall between endothelial cells.
The passive diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane.
Ingestion of large particulate debris or pathogens into phagosomes.

explanation: Endothelial cells contain numerous flask-shaped plasmalemmal vesicles (caveolae) on both their luminal and basal surfaces. These vesicles take up macromolecules (such as albumin, immunoglobulins, and lipoproteins) and transport them across the cell cytoplasm to the abluminal space in a process called transcytosis.
examTip: Continuous capillaries of skeletal muscle and lungs exhibit abundant transcytotic vesicles; in contrast, continuous capillaries of the blood-brain barrier have very few or no vesicles.

evidence.quote: These vesicles are responsible for transport of macromolecules in both directions across the endothelial cytoplasm. This process is called transcytosis.

stem: Which structural modification distinguishes continuous capillaries forming the blood-brain barrier (BBB) from ordinary continuous capillaries in skeletal muscle?

choices.text: Presence of continuous basal lamina with well-developed occluding tight junctions and virtually NO pinocytotic vesicles
choices.rationale: Brain continuous capillaries forming the BBB have prominent continuous tight junctions (zonula occludens) and extremely few or no pinocytotic vesicles, severely restricting transcellular macromolecular flux.

choices.text: Perforated basal lamina with open transendothelial channels
choices.rationale: Brain capillaries have an intact, uninterrupted continuous basal lamina.

choices.text: Presence of 60-80 nm fenestrations covered by diaphragms
choices.rationale: Brain capillaries are non-fenestrated; fenestrations would destroy the barrier function.

choices.text: Absence of pericytes and astrocytic end-feet
choices.rationale: Astrocytic end-feet encircle brain capillaries and induce BBB properties.

explanation: The blood-brain barrier is formed by modified continuous capillaries characterized by: 1) complex continuous occluding junctions (tight junctions) between adjacent endothelial cells, 2) continuous basal lamina, and 3) very few or absent pinocytotic vesicles, preventing non-specific vesicular transcytosis.
examTip: Breakdown of endothelial tight junctions in the BBB (e.g. by brain tumors or ischemia) causes vasogenic cerebral edema.

evidence.quote: In the brain, the blood capillaries are modified continuous capillaries that form the blood brain barrier, with very low permeability. Few or no pinocytotic vesicles are encountered in these continuous capillaries. • Occluding junction between endothelial cells represent the main structural component of the barrier.

stem: Which of the following organs features FENESTRATED capillaries characterized by transendothelial pores (60-80 nm) and a continuous basal lamina?

choices.text: Endocrine glands, small intestinal villi, and renal glomeruli
choices.rationale: Fenestrated capillaries are located in organs with rapid molecular exchange or filtration: endocrine glands, intestinal mucosa (nutrient absorption), and kidneys (glomerular filtration and peritubular capillaries).
These organs contain continuous capillaries.

choices.text: Liver, spleen, and red bone marrow
choices.rationale: These organs contain sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries.
Contains continuous non-fenestrated capillaries (BBB).

explanation: Fenestrated capillaries have transcellular pores (60-80 nm) through the endothelial cells that are typically bridged by a thin non-membranous proteoglycan diaphragm (except in renal glomeruli where diaphragms are absent). The basal lamina is continuous. They occur where rapid transport of fluids, hormones, or metabolites is required.
examTip: Fenestrated = endocrine, gut, kidneys; Continuous = muscle, lung, brain; Sinusoid = liver, spleen, bone marrow.

evidence.quote: Fenestrated capillaries : The endothelial cells have pores (60 -80 nm in diameter), and usually covered by a pore diaphragm. The basal lamina is continuous. They are present in endocrine glands, intestines, and the kidney glomeruli

stem: Under electron microscopy, which type of capillary exhibits wide intercellular gaps, an incomplete or absent basal lamina, and fenestrae that lack diaphragms to allow passage of entire cells?

choices.rationale: Continuous capillaries have unbroken basal lamina and tight occluding junctions.
Fenestrated capillaries maintain a continuous basal lamina and diaphragms across pores.

Sinusoids feature large tortuous lumina, intercellular gaps, fenestrations without diaphragms, and a discontinuous or absent basal lamina, facilitating migration of whole cells and large proteins in liver, spleen, and bone marrow.
Lymphatic capillaries lack fenestrae and have overlapping endothelial flaps.

explanation: Sinusoids (discontinuous capillaries) have wide irregular diameters (30-40 μm), open intercellular gaps between endothelial cells, absent or fragmented basal lamina, and fenestrations without diaphragms. Associated phagocytic macrophages (e.g. Kupffer cells in liver) often reside inside or along the wall.
examTip: Sinusoids in bone marrow and spleen allow newly manufactured blood cells to enter the general circulation directly.

evidence.quote: Sinusoidal capillaries, or sinusoids, can be found in the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. The endothelial wall and the basal lamina are discontinuous. The fenestrae in the endothelial cells are without diaphragm.

stem: Which histological specialization is characteristic of medium-sized cerebral (basilar) arteries compared to other systemic muscular arteries?

choices.text: A very thin tunica media devoid of elastic fibers, but with a well-developed internal elastic lamina
choices.rationale: Cerebral arteries are protected inside the skull from external forces; their tunica media is thin and lacks elastic fibers, but their internal elastic lamina is well developed.

choices.text: An exceptionally thick tunica adventitia containing skeletal muscle bundles
choices.rationale: Adventitia of cerebral arteries is extremely thin with no muscle.

choices.text: Complete absence of internal and external elastic laminae
choices.rationale: The internal elastic lamina is prominent and well developed.

choices.text: Multiple fenestrated capillaries embedded within the intima
choices.rationale: Normal artery walls do not contain intimal capillaries.

explanation: Cerebral arteries within the subarachnoid space are shielded by cerebrospinal fluid and the bony cranium from mechanical stresses. Consequently, their wall is thin, their media is thin and devoid of elastic fibers, but the internal elastic lamina is prominently developed.
examTip: Congenital defects in the muscular media at branch points of cerebral arteries predispose to berry (saccular) aneurysms in the Circle of Willis.

evidence.quote: 1.Cerebral (basilar) Arteries: They have thin wall because they are protected from external forces by skull. The tunica media is thin and devoid of elastic fibers. The internal elastic lamina is well developed.

stem: Why do the main coronary arteries have a remarkably thick wall and subendothelial layer containing longitudinal smooth muscle fibers and fat droplets under microscopic inspection?

choices.text: Because they are subjected to high pressure, twisting, and repetitive mechanical deformation during each cardiac cycle
choices.rationale: Subjected to high internal systolic pressures and repeated physical bending/compression during each myocardial contraction, coronary arteries have a thick intima with longitudinal smooth muscle and a reinforced media to withstand mechanical forces.

choices.text: Because they carry deoxygenated blood under low venous pressures
choices.rationale: Coronary arteries carry oxygenated arterial blood under systemic arterial pressure.

choices.text: Because they lack a muscular media entirely
choices.rationale: Their media is exceptionally thick.
