choices.text: Because they function as chemoreceptors regulating heart rate
choices.rationale: Chemoreceptors reside in carotid and aortic bodies.

explanation: Coronary arteries are muscular arteries subjected to unique hemodynamic stresses: high aortic driving pressure and severe cyclical mechanical twisting/compression by contracting myocardium. Histologically, their intima is physiologically thickened with longitudinal smooth muscle fibers and elastin, and their media is thick.
examTip: This unique thickened intima with longitudinal smooth muscle predisposes coronary arteries to accelerated atherosclerosis.

evidence.quote: Coronary Arteries: They have a very thick wall because they are subjected to high pressure. The intima is thickened. The sub endothelium contains longitudinal smooth muscle fibers, elastic fibers, amorphous intercellular substance, fat droplets and monocytes.

stem: What histological arrangement of the tunica media in the umbilical arteries enables their complete muscular constriction and physiological occlusion at birth?

choices.text: Two distinct smooth muscle layers: an inner longitudinal layer and an outer circular layer (with no internal elastic lamina)
choices.rationale: The umbilical arteries lack an internal elastic lamina; their media is composed of an inner longitudinal and outer circular layer of smooth muscle that violently contracts upon cold stimulus and oxygenation at birth to occlude the lumen.

choices.text: A single layer of striated muscle cells surrounding a fenestrated internal lamina
choices.rationale: Arteries contain smooth muscle, never skeletal/striated muscle.

choices.text: Multiple concentric lamellae of elastin with no smooth muscle cells
choices.rationale: Elastic arteries contain elastin lamellae; umbilical arteries are predominantly muscular.

choices.text: Loose connective tissue lacking any muscular tunic
choices.rationale: The umbilical artery media is thick and muscular.

explanation: The human umbilical artery has two unique features: 1) it lacks an internal elastic lamina, and 2) its thick muscular media is arranged into two discrete layers (inner longitudinal and outer circular). This cross-helical orientation provides powerful sphincter-like closure upon birth to prevent neonatal hemorrhage.
examTip: Normal umbilical cord contains TWO umbilical arteries and ONE umbilical vein (2A 1V) embedded in Wharton's jelly.

evidence.quote: 4. Umbilical Arteries: The tunica intima lacks internal elastic lamina. The tunica media is chiefly muscular. The muscle layer of the media is divided into 2 layers: an inner longitudinal and outer circular layer. This arrangement will enable the umbilical artery to undergo complete occlusion after birth.

concept: Carotid Sinus Histological Structure and Innervation
stem: Which histological features characterize the wall of the CAROTID SINUS to optimize its function as an arterial baroreceptor?

choices.text: A thinner tunica media that distends easily and a thicker adventitia heavily innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
choices.rationale: The carotid sinus wall has a thinner, more compliant media that stretches readily with elevated blood pressure, and a thick adventitia heavily supplied by sensory afferent endings of the glossopharyngeal nerve (nerve of Hering).

choices.text: A thick muscular media devoid of nerve endings that contracts vigorously
choices.rationale: The media is thin to promote passive stretching, not active contraction.

choices.text: Clusters of catecholamine-secreting glomus cells in the intima
choices.rationale: Glomus cells are found in the carotid body (chemoreceptor), not carotid sinus.

choices.text: An absent adventitia with direct pericardial coverage
choices.rationale: Carotid sinus has a thick adventitia in the neck, far from pericardium.

explanation: The carotid sinus is a localized dilatation of the internal carotid artery just above the bifurcation. Its wall is modified for baroreception: the media is thinner and more elastic to allow stretch during systolic pressure rises, and the adventitia is thickened and densely innervated by baroreceptor endings of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
examTip: Carotid sinus massage stretches baroreceptor endings, increasing CN IX afferent firing to the solitary nucleus, which increases vagal tone and slows the heart rate (used to terminate SVT).

evidence.quote: At the site of the carotid sinus, the adventitia of the internal carotid artery is relatively thicker and heavily supplied with sensory nerve ending from the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX). The media is thinner, so, it distends during increase in blood pressure.

stem: Which two cell populations comprise the parenchyma of the CAROTID BODY (chemoreceptor) located at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery?

choices.text: Glomus cells (chemoreceptor cells) and Sheath cells (supporting sustentacular cells)
choices.rationale: The carotid body consists of clusters of pale-staining Type I Glomus cells (chemoreceptors with dense-core vesicles) surrounded by Type II Sheath/sustentacular cells.
Cardiac conduction tissue, not peripheral vascular chemoreceptor.
General connective tissue and capillary cells.
Chromaffin cells are in adrenal medulla; parietal cells in stomach.

explanation: The carotid body contains clusters of Type I glomus cells (dopaminergic chemoreceptors) encapsulated by Type II sustentacular/sheath cells. Glomus cells depolarize in response to hypoxemia (low pO2), hypercapnia (high pCO2), and acidosis (low pH), releasing neurotransmitters to stimulate CN IX sensory fibers.
examTip: Carotid body = Chemoreceptor (O2, CO2, pH, via CN IX); Aortic body = Chemoreceptor (via CN X).

evidence.quote: Glomus cells :( chemoreceptor cells) and Sheath cells: (supporting cells). Function: It has specialized chemoreceptor nerve endings responsible for monitoring changes in O2 &CO2.

stem: Which endogenous vasodilator molecule is synthesized and released by vascular endothelial cells to relax underlying vascular smooth muscle?

choices.rationale: Vascular endothelial cells synthesize nitric oxide (endothelium-derived relaxing factor) via eNOS, which diffuses to smooth muscle cells to stimulate guanylyl cyclase, increase cGMP, and induce vasodilation.
Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor, not a vasodilator.
Platelet-derived vasoconstrictor and platelet aggregator.
Synthesized by plasma ACE action, potent systemic vasoconstrictor.

explanation: Endothelial cells secrete vasoactive substances that regulate local vasomotor tone: Nitric oxide (NO) and Prostacyclin (PGI2) promote relaxation, whereas Endothelin-1 and Angiotensin II promote smooth muscle contraction.
examTip: Endothelial dysfunction in atherosclerosis impairs nitric oxide production, causing paradoxical vasoconstriction and leukocyte adhesion.

evidence.quote: Functions of endothelial cells: 1- They provide smooth surface. 2- They secrete collagen, lamin, endothelin and nitric oxide. 3- They have membrane bound enzymes

concept: Internal Elastic Lamina in Arteries vs Veins
stem: Under light microscopy, a prominent scalloped (wavy) internal elastic membrane is clearly visible separating the tunica intima from the tunica media in which type of vessel?

choices.rationale: Muscular arteries display a distinct, well-defined, undulating (wavy) internal elastic lamina (IEL) separating the intima from the media, which is absent in veins.
Veins lack a well-developed internal elastic lamina, giving their intima a smooth contour.
Capillaries consist solely of endothelium, basal lamina, and pericytes without internal elastic membranes.
Venules have no elastic membranes.

explanation: In muscular arteries, the border between the tunica intima and tunica media is marked by a prominent internal elastic lamina (IEL). Upon fixation and contraction of smooth muscle, this elastic membrane forms characteristic wavy folds. Veins do not possess a distinct internal elastic membrane.
examTip: Wavy scalloped internal elastic lamina = Muscular artery; Smooth flat intima without IEL = Vein.

evidence.quote: The tunica intima of arteries appears wavy because of the elastic fibers below it. This “wrinkling” allows for stretching without excessive stress on the endothelial cell layer. In large arteries, there is also an additional layer of elastic fibers known as the internal elastic membrane. The internal elastic membrane is not present in veins.

stem: Why are the walls of the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries significantly thinner with less muscular and elastic tissue than the systemic aorta?

choices.text: Because pulmonary arterial circulation operates under low blood pressure (~25/10 mmHg) compared to systemic circulation (~120/80 mmHg)
choices.rationale: Pulmonary arterial pressure is approximately one-sixth of systemic aortic pressure; hence, the pulmonary arterial wall does not require the heavy elastic lamellae and muscular thickness seen in the aorta.

choices.text: Because they are protected by the rigid skull bones
choices.rationale: This applies to cerebral (basilar) arteries.

choices.text: Because they carry only lymphatic fluid rather than erythrocytes
choices.rationale: They carry whole blood to the pulmonary alveolar capillary bed.

choices.text: Because they lack endothelial cells and basement membrane
choices.rationale: All vessels possess an endothelial lining.

explanation: The pulmonary arterial tree operates under low hydrostatic pressure (mean pressure ~15 mmHg; systolic ~25 mmHg), compared to the high-pressure systemic aorta (mean pressure ~100 mmHg; systolic ~120 mmHg). Consequently, pulmonary arteries have thinner walls with fewer elastic lamellae and less smooth muscle.
examTip: In primary pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary arteries develop severe muscular hypertrophy and plexiform lesions in response to sustained high pressures.

evidence.quote: 2.Pulmonary Arteries: These vessels are thin walled, because they are exposed to low pulmonary blood pressure. They contain less muscular and elastic tissue.

concept: Streptococcal Pharyngitis vs Skin Infection in RF
stem: Which of the following clinical presentations of Streptococcus pyogenes infection is NOT a recognized trigger for the development of Acute Rheumatic Fever?

choices.rationale: Rheumatic fever develops strictly following streptococcal pharyngitis/tonsillitis, and is NEVER associated with cutaneous streptococcal infections like impetigo, erysipelas, or cellulitis (which trigger post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis instead).
Pharyngeal infection with GAS is the classic trigger for acute rheumatic fever.
Directly triggers acute rheumatic fever if untreated.
Scarlet fever is a pharyngeal GAS infection with erythrogenic toxin, predisposing to rheumatic fever.

explanation: Acute rheumatic fever is exclusively an autoimmune sequela of Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal (GAS) pharyngitis. Unlike post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), which occurs after both skin and pharyngeal infections, rheumatic fever is not associated with streptococcal skin infections (impetigo, pyoderma, erysipelas).
examTip: Pharyngitis triggers BOTH Rheumatic Fever and PSGN; Skin impetigo triggers ONLY PSGN, NEVER Rheumatic Fever.

evidence.quote: Rheumatic fever is not associated with streptococcal skin infections (e.g.,erysipelas, impetigo, cellulitis).

stem: What is the immunological mechanism responsible for carditis in Acute Rheumatic Fever?

choices.text: Type II hypersensitivity reaction where antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin
choices.rationale: Molecular mimicry occurs when antibodies generated against the alpha-helical coiled-coil structure of streptococcal M protein cross-react with structurally homologous human cardiac myosin and laminin, triggering immune-mediated cytotoxic damage (Type II hypersensitivity).

choices.text: Direct bacteremic invasion of myocardial cells by Streptococcus pyogenes
choices.rationale: Rheumatic fever is a non-suppurative sterile immune sequela; bacteria do not invade myocardium.

choices.text: Type III hypersensitivity complex deposition in myocardial capillaries
choices.rationale: Type III immune complex deposition occurs in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, not RF carditis.

choices.text: Superantigen-mediated massive release of interleukin-2 and TNF-alpha
choices.rationale: This is the mechanism of Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (STSS), not rheumatic fever.

explanation: Group A streptococcal M protein shares structural homology with human cardiac myosin and valve glycoproteins. In genetically susceptible individuals, anti-M protein antibodies cross-react with cardiac epitopes, activating complement and recruitment of CD4+ T lymphocytes (Type II hypersensitivity), producing pancarditis.
examTip: M protein is the chief virulence factor of S. pyogenes; it prevents phagocytosis and induces molecular mimicry.

evidence.quote: antibodies formed against M protein of Group A β-hemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) (GAS) may cross react with the heart tissues (myosin) and cause rheumatic fever→ type II hypersensitivity reaction

stem: Which of the following physical characteristics correctly describes the rash of ERYTHEMA MARGINATUM seen in Acute Rheumatic Fever?

choices.text: Transitional flat or barely raised, ring-like (annular) erythematous lesions on the trunk that are painless and non-pruritic
choices.rationale: Erythema marginatum consists of evanescent, non-pruritic, pink or red serpentine/ring-like macules with clear central margins located predominantly on the trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the face.

choices.text: Intensely pruritic vesicular eruption in a dermatomal distribution
choices.rationale: Describes Herpes zoster.

choices.text: Painful violaceous nodules located over the anterior shins
choices.rationale: Describes erythema nodosum.

choices.text: Sandpaper-like diffuse punctate rash on the face and neck
choices.rationale: Describes the rash of scarlet fever.

explanation: Erythema marginatum is a major Jones criterion seen in ~10% of acute rheumatic fever cases. It presents as non-pruritic, non-painful, ring-shaped or serpent-like pink macules with central clearing that rapidly appear, fade, and migrate across the trunk and proximal extremities.
examTip: Erythema marginatum is non-pruritic and never affects the face.

evidence.quote: Erythema marginatum : Transitional flat or barely raised ring-like lesion on trunk . Painless and non-pruritic.

stem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of rapid, uncoordinated, purposeless, jerky movements of her limbs and facial grimacing that disappear during sleep. What is this neurological manifestation of Acute Rheumatic Fever?

choices.rationale: Sydenham chorea is a major Jones criterion characterized by involuntary, non-repetitive, irregular choreiform movements and emotional lability resulting from autoimmune cross-reactivity against basal ganglia neurons.
Autosomal dominant trinucleotide repeat disease manifesting in adulthood.
Sustained tonic contractions and trismus caused by tetanospasmin toxin.
Chronic motor and vocal tics.

explanation: Sydenham chorea is a major manifestation of acute rheumatic fever that often appears late (up to 6 months after GAS pharyngitis). It is caused by anti-streptococcal antibodies cross-reacting with striatal gangliosides in the caudate and subthalamic nuclei.
examTip: Sydenham chorea may be the sole clinical manifestation of RF; in such cases, evidence of preceding GAS infection is not strictly required to make the diagnosis.

evidence.quote: Sydenham chorea: Involuntary, irregular, nonrepetitive movements of the limbs, neck, head, and/or face.

concept: ASO Titer Diagnostic Threshold and Kinetics
stem: Regarding serological confirmation of preceding GAS pharyngitis in Acute Rheumatic Fever, what Antistreptolysin O (ASO) antibody titer is considered confirmatory in clinical practice?

choices.text: 200 Todd units or more (peaking 3-6 weeks post-infection)
choices.rationale: An elevated ASO titer of >= 200 units (or > 1:400 Todd units) is confirmatory of recent GAS infection. ASO begins rising in 1 week and reaches maximum peak at 3-6 weeks post-infection.
This is a normal baseline negative value.

choices.text: 1000 Todd units only if accompanied by thrombocytopenia
choices.rationale: Thrombocytopenia is not a feature of RF.
Hepatitis B marker, unrelated to Streptococcus pyogenes.

explanation: Serum antistreptolysin O (ASO) titers rise 1-3 weeks following streptococcal infection, peak at 3-6 weeks, and decline over several months. An ASO titer >= 200 Todd units (or a four-fold increase in paired titers) confirms recent GAS exposure.
examTip: If ASO is negative or equivocal, anti-DNase B (which peaks at 6-8 weeks) is the most reliable second-line serologic test.

evidence.quote: A raised level of Antistreptolysin O (ASO) antibody titers (200 units or more) is CONFIRMATORY.

concept: Cause of Early Death in Acute Rheumatic Fever
stem: What is the primary cause of early cardiac mortality during the acute inflammatory phase of Acute Rheumatic Fever?

choices.text: Severe myocarditis causing acute heart failure or fatal arrhythmias
choices.rationale: During the acute episode, death is almost always attributable to acute rheumatic myocarditis (causing conduction blocks, malignant arrhythmias, or fulminant pump failure).

choices.text: Rupture of the sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
choices.rationale: Rare congenital or syphilitic complication, not the cause of early acute RF death.

choices.text: Massive pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis
choices.rationale: Not the primary acute RF complication.
Mitral stenosis develops chronically years to decades after the acute attack.

explanation: Although chronic rheumatic heart disease kills via progressive valvular scarring (mitral stenosis), death during the acute phase of rheumatic fever is primarily caused by diffuse rheumatic myocarditis, which disrupts the conduction system and impairs ventricular contractility.
examTip: Early death = Myocarditis; Late death/morbidity = Chronic valvular deformity (Mitral stenosis).

evidence.quote: Early death in rheumatic fever is usually due to myocarditis.

stem: What is the drug and dosing regimen of choice for secondary prevention of recurrent Acute Rheumatic Fever in a patient without penicillin allergy?

choices.text: Intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G administered every 28 days (4 weeks)
choices.rationale: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G (1.2 million units) every 28 days (or every 3-4 weeks) is the gold standard secondary prophylactic regimen to prevent recurrent GAS pharyngitis.
Fluoroquinolones are ineffective for streptococcal eradication and prophylaxis.
Vancomycin is reserved for severe MRSA hospital infections, not outpatient RF prophylaxis.
Tetracyclines are not indicated for secondary RF prophylaxis.

explanation: Recurrent episodes of GAS pharyngitis trigger recurrent rheumatic fever attacks, causing cumulative damage to heart valves. Long-term secondary prophylaxis with IM benzathine penicillin G every 28 days is mandatory to protect against recurrent infection.
examTip: In penicillin-allergic patients, oral macrolides (e.g. erythromycin or azithromycin) are used for secondary prophylaxis.

evidence.quote: Secondary prevention: Drug of choice: IM penicillin G benzathine. In patients with a penicillin allergy: oral macrolides. Usually administered every 28 days

stem: A 38-year-old male with a history of rheumatic mitral valve prolapse undergoes a dental extraction. Three weeks later, he develops low-grade fever, night sweats, and a new systolic murmur. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant, catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci in chains. Which pathogen is responsible?

choices.text: Viridans group streptococci (e.g. Streptococcus sanguinis, S. mutans)
choices.rationale: Viridans streptococci are normal commensals of the oral cavity that enter the bloodstream during dental manipulation and synthesize dextrans to adhere to damaged heart valves, causing subacute infective endocarditis.
S. pneumoniae is optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble, causing acute lobar pneumonia.
Catalase-positive, beta-hemolytic cocci in clusters; causes fulminant acute endocarditis.
Non-hemolytic or alpha-hemolytic; associated with genitourinary or GI procedures.

explanation: Viridans streptococci are the most common cause of subacute bacterial endocarditis in native valves with preexisting architectural defects (rheumatic disease, MVP). Transient bacteremia caused by toothbrushing or dental scaling allows these oral flora to produce extracellular dextrans that bind to fibrin-platelet clots.
examTip: Viridans = Subacute, damaged valves, dental work; S. aureus = Acute, native valves, IV drug users.

evidence.quote: Etiology: The condition is a result of bacteremia, which is most commonly caused by dental procedures, surgery, distant primary infections, and non-sterile injections.

concept: Right-Sided IE in Intravenous Drug Abuse
stem: A 26-year-old intravenous heroin user presents with high spiking fevers, cough, pleuritic chest pain, and multiple cavitary nodular infiltrates on chest CT. Blood cultures grow beta-hemolytic, catalase-positive, coagulase-positive Gram-positive cocci. Which cardiac valve and organism are most likely involved?

choices.rationale: Intravenous drug use is strongly associated with acute right-sided infective endocarditis involving the tricuspid valve, predominantly caused by virulent Staphylococcus aureus. Friable vegetations embolize into the pulmonary circulation, causing septic pulmonary infarcts.
Mitral involvement with viridans presents as subacute left-sided IE with systemic emboli.
Causes left-sided endocarditis following GU procedures.
Fungal endocarditis is less common and tricuspid valve is far more frequently affected than pulmonary.

explanation: Skin contamination during non-sterile intravenous drug injection introduces Staphylococcus aureus directly into venous return. The tricuspid valve is exposed first and bears the brunt of the bacterial load, producing acute right-sided IE characterized by high fevers, holosystolic regurgitant murmur, and septic pulmonary emboli.
examTip: Remember: 'Don't TRI drugs' (Tricuspid valve affected in IV drug users; organism is S. aureus).
mnemonic: Don't TRI drugs (Tricuspid = IV drug use)

evidence.quote: Tricuspid valve disease is associated with intravenous (IV) drug use. Staphylococcus aureus, HACEK, Candida

stem: Two months after receiving a mechanical aortic valve replacement, a 65-year-old man develops persistent fever and bacteremia. Blood cultures grow novobiocin-sensitive, coagulase-negative staphylococci. What is the most likely pathogen?

choices.rationale: Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative) is the leading cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis (<12 months post-surgery), introduced perioperatively and forming durable biofilms on synthetic valve sewing rings.
Novobiocin-resistant, causes uncomplicated urinary tract infections in young women.
Associated with underlying colorectal adenocarcinoma.
Gram-negative bacillus.

explanation: Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (<1 year after surgery) is most frequently caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase-negative staphylococci). These organisms produce an extracellular polysaccharide slime (biofilm) that protects them from host phagocytes and antibiotics.
examTip: Early prosthetic valve IE (<1 year) = S. epidermidis (biofilm); Late prosthetic valve IE (>1 year) = Viridans streptococci (resembles native valve).

evidence.quote: Preexisting valvular endothelial damage or prosthetic valves predispose to bacterial colonization, especially of those that cause subacute IE

stem: Which peripheral cutaneous finding in Infective Endocarditis presents as PAINFUL, tender, erythematous nodules on the pads of the fingers and toes due to immune complex deposition?

choices.rationale: Osler nodes are painful, tender erythematous nodules located on the pulp of fingers and toes caused by immune complex-mediated microvascular inflammation.
Janeway lesions are painless, non-tender flat macules on the palms and soles caused by septic microemboli.
Retinal hemorrhages with pale centers viewed on fundoscopy.
Linear subungual dark streaks under nail beds.

explanation: Osler nodes are painful, purpuric, palpable nodules on the fingers and toes caused by immune complex deposition (Type III hypersensitivity). In contrast, Janeway lesions are painless, erythematous, non-tender macules on the palms and soles caused by septic emboli containing viable bacteria.
examTip: O-sler nodes hurt: 'O = Ouch! (painful)'. Janeway = Jane is gentle / no pain (painless).

evidence.quote: Clinical features:include constitutional symptoms (fatigue, fever/chills, malaise) in combination with signs of pathological cardiac changes (e.g., new or changed heart murmur, heart failure signs) and possibly manifestations of subsequent damage to other organs

concept: Blood Culture Collection Protocol for IE
stem: What is the standard blood culture collection protocol to establish the microbiological diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis?

choices.text: Three separate sets of blood cultures drawn from different venipuncture sites, with the first and last samples obtained at least 1 hour apart, prior to starting antibiotics
choices.rationale: Endocarditis involves continuous endovascular bacteremia. Three sets drawn at least 1 hour apart from different peripheral venipuncture sites before antimicrobial therapy allow recovery of cultivable pathogens and prove continuous bacteremia.

choices.text: A single blood culture bottle drawn from an indwelling central venous catheter
choices.rationale: A single culture or catheter draw is prone to contamination and does not prove persistent bacteremia.

choices.text: Daily blood draws after 7 days of broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
choices.rationale: Cultures must be obtained before initiating antimicrobial therapy to avoid sterile false negatives.

choices.text: Urine cultures and throat swabs only
choices.rationale: Endocarditis requires documentation of persistent bloodstream infection.

explanation: Because endocarditis vegetations continuously shed bacteria into the bloodstream, standard diagnostic criteria require three sets of blood cultures collected from distinct peripheral venipuncture sites, with at least 1 hour between the first and last collection, before initiating intravenous antibiotics.
examTip: A single positive blood culture is insufficient to confirm IE, as it frequently reflects cutaneous contamination.

evidence.quote: Three sets of blood cultures are collected from different sites with the first and last samples drawn at least 1 hour apart. Standardblood culture of 5 days period allows recovery of most cultivable microorganisms including Candida and the fastidious HACEK organisms. Most (usually all) blood cultures from endocarditis patients caused by cultivable organisms should be positive. A single positive blood culture doesNOT typically represent endocarditis pathogen.

stem: Which of the following is the most frequent clinical cause of 'Culture-Negative Endocarditis' where echocardiography shows vegetations but routine 5-day blood cultures remain sterile?

choices.text: Recent administration of antimicrobial therapy prior to blood collection
choices.rationale: Prior antibiotic treatment is the single most common cause of culture-negative endocarditis, rapidly suppressing bacterial replication in blood while viable organisms remain deep in the vegetation.
S. aureus grows rapidly and easily in standard blood culture media.
Troponin does not sterilize blood cultures.
Candida grows in standard modern blood culture systems.

explanation: Culture-negative endocarditis (CNE) refers to cases where clinical/echocardiographic criteria for IE are met, but blood cultures yield no growth. The predominant cause is prior empiric antibiotic therapy. Other causes include fastidious or intracellular organisms: Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella, Tropheryma whipplei, and HACEK group.
examTip: In suspected culture-negative IE, PCR amplification of bacterial 16S rRNA and serology for Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) are the diagnostic tests of choice.

evidence.quote: CNE might be caused by: recent administration of antimicrobial therapy,intracellular organisms as Coxiella burnetii & Bartonella spp or fastidious organisms.

stem: Which of the following virological characteristics correctly describes Coxsackievirus B, the leading viral pathogen causing myocarditis?

choices.text: Positive-sense, single-stranded, linear RNA virus with a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid (Picornaviridae family)
choices.rationale: Coxsackievirus B is a member of the Enterovirus genus in the Picornaviridae family; it is a non-enveloped, icosahedral capsid virus containing a single-stranded positive-sense (+)ssRNA genome.

choices.text: Enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus with helical symmetry
choices.rationale: Describes Herpesviridae, not Coxsackievirus.
Describes Orthomyxoviridae (influenza).

choices.text: Non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus with icosahedral capsid
choices.rationale: Describes Parvovirus B19.

explanation: Coxsackievirus B belongs to the genus Enterovirus within the family Picornaviridae ('pico' = small, 'RNA' = RNA genome). It is non-enveloped, has an icosahedral capsid, and possesses a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome that can directly serve as mRNA.
examTip: Coxsackievirus B is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and binds to the CAR (coxsackievirus-adenovirus receptor) on cardiomyocytes.

evidence.quote: Coxsackievirus B: most common virus causing myocarditis. An enterovirus that belongs to the Picorna viridae family. Non-enveloped, icosahedral capsid, linear, single-stranded, positive sense RNA virus

concept: Sudden Death in Young Adults & Viral Myocarditis
stem: In approximately what percentage of sudden, unexplained cardiac deaths in young adults is myocarditis diagnosed on post-mortem histopathological examination?

choices.rationale: Myocarditis is an inflammatory disorder that disproportionately strikes adolescents and young athletes, accounting for approximately 10% of sudden unexpected cardiac deaths at post-mortem evaluation.
Significantly underestimates the prevalence of myocarditis in young sudden deaths.
Too high; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and anomalous coronaries also contribute.

choices.text: Exclusively in elderly patients over age 80
choices.rationale: Myocarditis characteristically affects children, adolescents, and young adults.

explanation: Viral myocarditis is a leading cause of sudden death in young adults and athletes (<35 years of age). In post-mortem autopsies of young sudden cardiac deaths, active lymphomonocytic myocarditis is identified in ~10% of cases.
examTip: Young patient with recent flulike illness presenting with collapse, chest pain, or arrhythmias = suspect viral myocarditis.

evidence.quote: In ∼ 10% of sudden deaths in young adults, myocarditis is diagnosed in the post-mortem examination.

stem: While most adult patients with viral myocarditis make a complete recovery, what chronic myocardial condition can develop in a subset of patients due to persistent viral replication or autoimmune myocyte destruction?

choices.rationale: Chronic viral persistence and secondary autoimmune destruction of contractile tissue lead to ventricular wall thinning, 4-chamber dilatation, and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) with systolic heart failure.
HOCM is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder of sarcomeric proteins.
Non-atherosclerotic vascular disease, not a sequela of viral myocarditis.
Age-related degenerative calcification or bicuspid valve wear.

explanation: In 10-20% of patients with acute viral myocarditis, chronic inflammation and myocyte loss induce ventricular remodeling, chamber dilation, and impaired systolic function, ultimately manifesting as dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) requiring heart transplantation.
examTip: Viral myocarditis is the most common identifiable infectious trigger for acquired dilated cardiomyopathy.

evidence.quote: Whereas most adults with viral myocarditis make a full recovery, there is a small risk of the condition progressing to dilated cardiomyopathy.

stem: A 22-year-old collegiate athlete presents with sudden onset retrosternal chest pain and dyspnea 10 days after a flulike illness with fever and gastroenteritis. ECG shows diffuse ST elevations. Which laboratory finding confirms acute myocardial injury in this patient?

choices.text: Elevated serum cardiac troponin I/T and CK-MB levels
choices.rationale: Myocyte necrosis in active viral myocarditis releases cardiac-specific enzymes into the blood, producing marked elevations in serum troponin I/T and CK-MB, often mimicking acute coronary syndrome in young patients.
Marker of biliary or bone disease.
ESR and CRP are significantly elevated due to systemic inflammation.
Not a characteristic marker of acute myocarditis.

explanation: Viral myocarditis frequently presents in young patients as pseudo-infarction: acute chest pain, ECG ST-segment elevation, and elevated cardiac enzymes (troponin I/T and CK-MB). Normal coronary arteries on angiography confirm that myocyte necrosis is non-ischemic.
examTip: Troponin elevation in myocarditis indicates ongoing active inflammatory myocyte lysis.

evidence.quote: Non-specific blood tests: ↑ Cardiac enzymes, ↑ ESR & CRP, Leukocytosis or lymphocytosis

stem: A 72-year-old man develops Enterococcus faecalis infective endocarditis. Which preceding clinical intervention or condition is most characteristically associated with enterococcal bacteremia and endocarditis?

choices.text: Recent genitourinary instrumentation (e.g. cystoscopy, prostatectomy) or gastrointestinal surgery
choices.rationale: Enterococci (E. faecalis and E. faecium) are normal inhabitants of the GI and genitourinary flora. Endocarditis classically follows GU manipulations (cystoscopy, urinary catheterization) or obstetric/GI procedures in elderly men.
Associated with Viridans group streptococci.

choices.text: Intravenous heroin injection in a young person
choices.rationale: Classically associated with Staphylococcus aureus.

choices.text: Tick bite in an endemic forest area
choices.rationale: Associated with Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme carditis).

explanation: Enterococci are hardy, bile-resistant and salt-tolerant Gram-positive cocci in chains that colonize the colon and lower urinary tract. Enterococcal endocarditis characteristically affects older men undergoing urological procedures (transurethral resection, Foley catheterization) or patients with enterococcal UTIs.
examTip: Elderly man + urinary tract procedure / cystoscopy + new heart murmur = Enterococcus faecalis endocarditis.

evidence.quote: The condition is a result of bacteremia, which is most commonly caused by dental procedures, surgery, distant primary infections, and non-sterile injections.

stem: According to contemporary clinical guidelines, for which patient subset is antimicrobial prophylaxis specifically indicated prior to invasive dental procedures involving gingival manipulation?

choices.text: Patients with prosthetic heart valves, prior history of infective endocarditis, or unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease
choices.rationale: Current guidelines recommend antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. oral amoxicillin 2g 30-60 min prior) only for high-risk patients: prosthetic valves/material, prior IE, unrepaired cyanotic CHD, or repaired CHD with residual defects.

choices.text: All patients undergoing routine dental cleaning regardless of cardiac history
choices.rationale: Prophylaxis is restricted strictly to high-risk cardiac patients.

choices.text: Patients with uncomplicated physiological innocent murmurs
choices.rationale: Innocent functional murmurs carry zero risk of endocarditis.

choices.text: Patients with coronary artery disease without valvular lesions
choices.rationale: Atherosclerotic CAD without valvular disease is not an indication for IE prophylaxis.

explanation: Infective endocarditis prophylaxis is restricted to patients with the highest risk of adverse outcomes from endocarditis undergoing dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue: 1) Prosthetic cardiac valves or prosthetic material, 2) Previous infective endocarditis, 3) Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease.
examTip: Prophylaxis of choice: Oral Amoxicillin 2 grams single dose given 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure.

evidence.quote: Prophylaxis:Antibiotics are only administered in specific circumstances, e.g., in patients with preexisting heart conditions undergoing dental or surgical procedures.

concept: PCR Detection of Streptococcus pyogenes Gene
stem: Which specific streptococcal virulence gene is targeted in PCR-based assays for early, precise molecular diagnosis of Streptococcus pyogenes in suspected rheumatic heart disease?

choices.rationale: PCR assays targeting the conserved streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (speB) gene provide rapid, precise identification of GAS, assisting in early diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease.
Confers methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).
Confers vancomycin resistance in Enterococci (VRE).
Staphylococcal penicillin-binding protein.

explanation: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays detecting the speB (streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B) gene offer high analytical sensitivity and specificity, overcoming the delays of serology to confirm Streptococcus pyogenes infection in patients with acute rheumatic fever.
examTip: speB = Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin B (cysteine protease produced by almost all S. pyogenes strains).

evidence.quote: 5. PCR based diagnosis assay: Is used for identifying the Streptococcus pyrogenic exotoxin B gene. PCR-based diagnosis is more exact than serology and it also helps in early diagnosis of rheumatic heart disease.

stem: Blood flows from the right ventricle to the lungs through which valve?

choices.rationale: The mitral valve regulates flow between the left atrium and left ventricle.
The pulmonary semilunar valve guards the exit of the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk leading to the lungs.
The aortic valve regulates blood flow from the left ventricle into the ascending aorta.
The tricuspid valve regulates inflow from the right atrium into the right ventricle.

explanation: Blood deoxygenated in systemic tissues enters the right ventricle via the tricuspid orifice and is pumped during ventricular systole through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary trunk for oxygenation in the lungs.
examTip: Semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) guard the ventricular outflows, whereas atrioventricular valves guard the inflows.

evidence.quote: Blood flows from the right ventricle to the lungs through which valve? B. Pulmonary valve

stem: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium?

choices.rationale: Four pulmonary veins (two superior, two inferior) convey freshly oxygenated blood from the pulmonary capillaries to the left atrium.
The pulmonary arteries transport deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
The superior and inferior venae cavae transport systemic deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.
The aorta distributes oxygenated blood from the left ventricle to the entire systemic circulation.

explanation: Pulmonary veins are unique among veins in the postnatal body because they carry fully oxygenated blood from the alveolar capillary beds into the smooth-walled sinus venarum of the left atrium.
examTip: Pulmonary veins = Oxygenated to Left Atrium; Pulmonary arteries = Deoxygenated to Lungs.

evidence.quote: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium? A. Pulmonary vein

stem: Which heart valve allows blood to flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle?

choices.rationale: The mitral (bicuspid) atrioventricular valve guards the left atrioventricular orifice, opening in diastole to permit ventricular filling.
The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle.
The aortic valve guards the left ventricular outflow tract into the aorta.
The pulmonary valve guards the right ventricular outflow tract into the pulmonary trunk.

explanation: The mitral (bicuspid) valve consists of anterior and posterior cusps anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles in the left ventricle, permitting unidirection flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle.
examTip: Mitral/Bicuspid is on the left ('LAMB': Left Atrium Mitral Bicuspid); Tricuspid is on the right ('RAT': Right Atrium Tricuspid).

evidence.quote: Which heart valve allows blood to flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle? A. Mitral valve

concept: Systemic Venous Inflow via Vena Cava
stem: Which vessel returns mixed venous blood to the right atrium?

choices.rationale: The aorta receives blood ejected from the left ventricle and carries it to the systemic tissues.
Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the left atrium.
The superior vena cava (draining head, neck, upper limbs) and inferior vena cava (draining abdomen and lower limbs) return mixed systemic venous blood to the right atrium.
The pulmonary artery arises from the right ventricle and conveys blood to the pulmonary circulation.

explanation: Venous return from the supradiaphragmatic systemic circulation enters via the superior vena cava, while the infradiaphragmatic venous return enters via the inferior vena cava, both terminating in the right atrium.
examTip: Remember that the coronary sinus also empties venous blood from the myocardium itself directly into the right atrium.

evidence.quote: Which vessel returns mixed venous blood to the right atrium? C. Vena cava

stem: The tricuspid valve regulates blood flow between which two chambers?

choices.rationale: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve, positioned between the right atrium and right ventricle.
The mitral valve regulates flow between the left atrium and left ventricle.
The pulmonary semilunar valve controls outflow between the right ventricle and pulmonary artery.
The aortic semilunar valve controls outflow between the left ventricle and the aorta.

explanation: The tricuspid valve possesses three cusps (anterior, posterior, and septal) that separate the right atrium from the right ventricle, preventing backflow into the right atrium during right ventricular systole.
examTip: Tricuspid valve = 3 cusps on the right; Mitral valve = 2 cusps on the left.

evidence.quote: The tricuspid valve regulates blood flow between which two chambers? A. Right atrium and right ventricle

stem: Which structure separates the right and left sides of the heart?

choices.rationale: The external atrial wall forms the outer border of the chambers rather than partitioning left and right sides.
Valve leaflets prevent retrograde flow between atria and ventricles or between ventricles and great arteries.
The interatrial and interventricular muscular septa divide the heart longitudinally into right and left functional halves.
The pericardium is the fibroserous sac that surrounds and protects the entire heart.

explanation: The heart is partitioned into right (pulmonary) and left (systemic) functional pumps by an internal muscular and membranous partition consisting of the interatrial septum and interventricular septum.
examTip: The interventricular septum has both a thick muscular portion and a thin superior membranous portion (most common site of VSD).

evidence.quote: Which structure separates the right and left sides of the heart? C. Muscular septum

stem: What is the main role of the right side of the heart?

choices.rationale: Pumping blood to systemic tissues is the function of the high-pressure left side of the heart.
The right heart receives deoxygenated systemic venous return and propels it through the low-resistance pulmonary circuit to the lungs.
Renal blood flow is delivered through branches of the systemic aorta fed by the left heart.
Hepatic arterial blood flow originates from the systemic aorta; portal blood flow originates from splanchnic viscera.

explanation: The right ventricle acts as a volume pump operating at low pressures (systolic ~25 mmHg) designed specifically to overcome the low vascular resistance of the pulmonary arterial bed and perfuse the lungs for gas exchange.
examTip: Right ventricle = low-pressure volume pump for pulmonary bed; Left ventricle = high-pressure resistance pump for systemic circulation.

evidence.quote: What is the main role of the right side of the heart? B. Pump to lungs

stem: What type of blood enters the right side of the heart?

choices.rationale: Freshly oxygenated blood from the pulmonary capillaries enters the left atrium.
Although mesenteric venous blood contains nutrients, systemic mixed venous blood in the venae cavae is fundamentally deoxygenated.
Systemic venous blood returning to the right atrium and ventricle has surrendered oxygen to peripheral tissues (venous O2 saturation ~70-75%).
Central venous pressure entering the right heart is low (~0-4 mmHg), not high pressure.

explanation: Systemic tissues extract oxygen from arterial blood, returning mixed venous blood with reduced oxygen content and elevated carbon dioxide via the venae cavae into the right heart chambers.
examTip: Normal mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) in the right atrium/ventricle is approximately 70-75%.

evidence.quote: What type of blood enters the right side of the heart? C. Low oxygen blood

stem: What is the main function of the left side of the heart?

choices.rationale: Pumping to the lungs is the role of the right ventricle.
The left ventricle generates high systolic pressure (~120 mmHg) to distribute oxygenated blood through the aorta to all systemic organ systems.
The spleen is just one of many peripheral organs supplied by the systemic arterial tree.
The stomach receives blood via the celiac trunk, a sub-branch of the systemic aorta.

explanation: The left ventricle is a thick-walled, high-pressure muscular pump that ejects oxygen-rich blood into the aorta against systemic vascular resistance to perfuse all peripheral organs and tissues of the body.
examTip: Left ventricular wall is ~3 times thicker than the right ventricular wall due to higher afterload in the systemic circuit.

evidence.quote: What is the main function of the left side of the heart? B. Pump to body

stem: Which valves separate the atria from the ventricles?

choices.rationale: The aortic valve is a semilunar valve separating the left ventricle from the aorta.
The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve separating the right ventricle from the pulmonary trunk.
Atrioventricular (AV) valves—namely the tricuspid and mitral valves—physically and functionally separate the atria from the ventricles.
Semilunar (SL) valves separate the ventricular outflow tracts from the great arteries.

explanation: The atrioventricular (AV) valves comprise the tricuspid valve on the right and the bicuspid (mitral) valve on the left, preventing regurgitation of blood from ventricles back into atria during ventricular systole.
examTip: AV valves prevent backflow into atria during systole; SL valves prevent backflow into ventricles during diastole.

evidence.quote: Which valves separate the atria from the ventricles? C. AV valves

stem: Which valve is located on the right side between atrium and ventricle?

choices.rationale: The mitral valve is located on the left side between the left atrium and left ventricle.
The aortic valve is located between the left ventricle and aorta.
The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve positioned between the right atrium and right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve is located at the root of the pulmonary trunk.

explanation: The right atrioventricular orifice is guarded by the tricuspid valve, so called because it normally possesses three distinct leaflets: anterior, posterior, and septal.
examTip: Remember: Right = Tricuspid (3 leaflets); Left = Mitral/Bicuspid (2 leaflets).

evidence.quote: Which valve is located on the right side between atrium and ventricle? C. Tricuspid valve

stem: Which valves open during ventricular systole?

choices.rationale: Semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves open during the ejection phase of ventricular systole as intraventricular pressures exceed arterial pressures.
AV valves close at the onset of ventricular systole (producing S1) to prevent backward flow into the atria.
Venous valves in peripheral veins prevent venous reflux, independent of ventricular systole.
Lymphatic valves govern unidirectional lymph flow, not cardiac cycle ejection.

explanation: During ventricular isovolumetric contraction, pressure builds until ventricular pressure exceeds diastolic pressure in the aorta (80 mmHg) and pulmonary artery (10 mmHg), forcing open the semilunar valves for rapid ejection.
examTip: During systole: AV valves are CLOSED, Semilunar valves are OPEN. During diastole: AV valves are OPEN, Semilunar valves are CLOSED.

evidence.quote: Which valves open during ventricular systole? A. SL valves

stem: Which statement correctly compares the wall thickness of arteries and veins?

choices.text: Arteries have thinner walls and less muscle than veins
choices.rationale: Arteries have substantially thicker, muscular, and elastic walls compared to corresponding veins.

choices.text: Arteries have thicker, more elastic walls than veins
choices.rationale: Arteries possess a well-developed tunica media rich in vascular smooth muscle and elastic lamellae to withstand and buffer high systolic pressures.

choices.text: Veins have the thickest smooth muscle layer of all vessels
choices.rationale: Veins have a relatively thin tunica media and a thicker tunica adventitia.

choices.text: Veins have thicker walls to withstand high pressure
choices.rationale: Veins are low-pressure capacitance vessels and therefore have thin, easily distensible walls.

explanation: Arteries must withstand high and pulsatile systemic pressures, requiring thick walls with abundant elastin (elastic arteries) and smooth muscle (muscular arteries). In contrast, veins operate under low hydrostatic pressures and feature thin, collapsible walls.
examTip: Arteries = thick media, narrow round lumen; Veins = thin media, wide irregular collapsible lumen with valves.

evidence.quote: Which statement correctly compares the wall thickness of arteries and veins? B. Arteries have thicker, more elastic walls than veins

stem: Which option correctly describes the lumen size difference between arteries and veins?

choices.text: Arteries have a wider lumen than veins
choices.rationale: For an equivalent overall vascular caliber, arteries have a much narrower internal lumen due to their thick muscular wall.

choices.text: Veins have a narrower lumen to prevent backflow
choices.rationale: Veins have wide lumens; backflow prevention is achieved via endothelial valve cusps.
Veins have a noticeably larger lumen and thinner walls than their paired companion arteries, accommodating large capacitance volumes.

choices.text: Both arteries and veins have equal lumen diameters
choices.rationale: Veins accommodate over 60-70% of total blood volume, reflecting substantially wider lumina than companion arteries.

explanation: Because veins function as the primary blood reservoirs (capacitance vessels), their luminal cross-sectional area is substantially greater than that of companion arteries, offering low vascular resistance.
examTip: Companion vessel histology: Artery = narrow lumen, thick circular wall; Vein = large, often collapsed lumen, thin wall.

evidence.quote: Which option correctly describes the lumen size difference between arteries and veins? C. Veins have a wider lumen

stem: Which choice accurately describes the direction of blood flow in arteries versus veins?

choices.text: Arteries carry blood toward the heart; veins carry it away
choices.rationale: This reverses the foundational definition of arteries and veins.

choices.text: Both arteries and veins carry blood in the same direction
choices.rationale: Arteries and veins carry blood in opposite directions relative to the central cardiac pump.

choices.text: Arteries carry blood away from heart; veins carry it toward heart
choices.rationale: By physiological and anatomical definition, arteries distribute blood away from the cardiac ventricles, whereas veins return blood toward the atria.

choices.text: Veins and arteries alternate roles depending on pressure
choices.rationale: Vascular flow direction is structurally fixed by cardiac valve gating and pressure gradients.

explanation: Regardless of whether blood is oxygenated or deoxygenated, the anatomical definition of an artery is a vessel conducting blood away from the heart, while a vein conducts blood toward the heart.
examTip: Rule of thumb: A = Artery = Away from heart. Vein = Visiting the heart.

evidence.quote: Which choice accurately describes the direction of blood flow in arteries versus veins? C. Arteries carry blood away from heart; veins carry it toward heart

stem: Which statement best compares pressure characteristics in arteries and veins?

choices.text: Arteries operate at low, steady pressure; veins at high pulsatile pressure
choices.rationale: This is the exact opposite of true circulatory hemodynamic pressure profiles.

choices.text: Veins operate at high, pulsatile pressure; arteries at low steady pressure
choices.rationale: Veins are low-pressure non-pulsatile vessels, whereas arteries experience high pulsatile pressures.

choices.text: Both vessels experience the same pressure due to cardiac output
choices.rationale: Frictional resistance along arterioles dampens pressure and abolishes pulsatility before blood enters venules.

choices.text: Arteries have high, pulsatile pressure; veins have low, non-pulsatile pressure
choices.rationale: Arteries experience intermittent systolic ejection producing high, pulsatile pressure waves (e.g. 120/80 mmHg), while venous pressure is low (~2-10 mmHg) and non-pulsatile.

explanation: Intermittent ventricular ejection into the compliant aorta produces a high-pressure pulsatile wave. By the time blood traverses high-resistance systemic arterioles and capillary beds, pulsatility is dampened and pressure drops significantly, resulting in steady, low-pressure venous flow.
examTip: Pulse pressure is maximal in large arteries and drops to near zero at the capillary and venous levels.

evidence.quote: Which statement best compares pressure characteristics in arteries and veins? D. Arteries have high, pulsatile pressure; veins have low, non-pulsatile pressure

concept: Vascular Oxygen Carriage and Functional Role
stem: Which option correctly identifies the typical oxygen content and function of arteries versus veins?

choices.text: Arteries carry deoxygenated blood and act as reservoirs; veins distribute oxygenated blood
choices.rationale: Systemic arteries carry oxygenated blood to tissues, whereas veins serve as blood volume reservoirs.

choices.text: Both arteries and veins mainly carry oxygenated blood for systemic circulation
choices.rationale: Veins returning from tissues carry deoxygenated blood depleted of oxygen.

choices.text: Arteries are usually oxygenated and maintain systemic pressure; veins are usually deoxygenated and act as reservoirs
choices.rationale: In systemic circulation, arteries convey oxygenated blood under pressure to maintain organ perfusion, whereas systemic veins transport deoxygenated blood and act as high-capacitance reservoirs.

choices.text: Veins are oxygenated except pulmonary veins; arteries are deoxygenated except coronary arteries
choices.rationale: The classic exception is the pulmonary circulation: pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood, and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood.

explanation: In the systemic circulation, arteries convey oxygen-rich blood away from the left heart to supply metabolic demands while resisting pressure collapse. Veins contain deoxygenated blood and possess high capacitance, holding about two-thirds of the systemic blood volume.
examTip: Systemic: Arteries = oxygenated / pressure conduits; Veins = deoxygenated / volume reservoirs. (Reversed in pulmonary circuit).

evidence.quote: Which option correctly identifies the typical oxygen content and function of arteries versus veins? C. Arteries are usually oxygenated and maintain systemic pressure; veins are usually deoxygenated and act as reservoirs

stem: Which of the following represents the correct sequence of electrical impulse propagation through the cardiac conduction system from its site of origin to the ventricles?

choices.text: SA Node → AV Node → Atrial Internodal Pathways → Purkinje Fibers → Bundle Branches → Bundle of His
choices.rationale: Internodal pathways precede the AV node, and the Bundle of His precedes bundle branches and Purkinje fibers.

choices.text: SA Node → Atrial Internodal Pathways → AV Node → Bundle of His → Right & Left Bundle Branches → Purkinje Fibers
choices.rationale: Normal cardiac conduction originates in the SA node, traverses internodal pathways to the AV node, crosses through the Bundle of His into right and left bundle branches, and terminates in Purkinje subendocardial fibers.

choices.text: AV Node → SA Node → Bundle of His → Bundle Branches → Purkinje Fibers → Internodal Pathways
choices.rationale: The SA node, not the AV node, is the primary pacemaker and physiological site of origin.

choices.text: SA Node → Bundle of His → AV Node → Purkinje Fibers → Bundle Branches → Internodal Pathways
choices.rationale: The impulse must pass through the AV node before reaching the penetrating Bundle of His.

explanation: The physiological sequence of cardiac excitation begins at the SA node (highest intrinsic rate), travels across the atria via internodal pathways, pauses at the AV node (conduction delay), travels down the bundle of His, bifurcates into bundle branches, and spreads rapidly through the Purkinje arborization to activate ventricular myocardium from endocardium to epicardium.
examTip: Memory order: SA Node → Internodal tracts → AV Node → Bundle of His → Bundle Branches → Purkinje Fibers.

evidence.quote: Arrange the components of the cardiac conduction system in correct sequence from origin to ventricles: 1. Sinoatrial (SA) Node 2. Atrial Internodal Pathways 3. Atrioventricular (AV) Node 4. Bundle of His (AV Bundle) 5. Right & Left Bundle Branches 6. Purkinje Fibers

concept: Conduction Component Anatomical and Functional Characteristics
stem: Which component of the cardiac conduction system is correctly matched with its anatomical location and functional velocity feature?

choices.text: SA Node — Located in the superior wall of right atrium near SVC opening; serves as primary pacemaker with intrinsic rate 60–100 bpm
choices.rationale: The sinoatrial node is situated subepicardially at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium, exhibiting the steepest phase 4 prepotential slope to pace the heart.

choices.text: AV Node — Fastest conduction velocity (~2–4 m/s) ensuring synchronous ventricular depolarization
choices.rationale: The AV node has the slowest conduction velocity (~0.05 m/s); Purkinje fibers possess the fastest velocity.

choices.text: Bundle of His — Slows conduction velocity (~0.05 m/s) to delay ventricular filling
choices.rationale: The AV node provides the physiologic delay; the Bundle of His conducts rapidly (~1-2 m/s).

choices.text: Purkinje Fibers — Located in superior wall of right atrium near opening of superior vena cava
choices.rationale: Purkinje fibers form a subendocardial plexus in the ventricular myocardium, not in the right atrium.

choices.text: AV nodal delay prevents tetanic contraction, while Purkinje fibers slow ventricular emptying
choices.rationale: Tetanus prevention is due to the prolonged plateau and refractory period, not the AV nodal delay.

choices.text: AV nodal delay allows sufficient time for complete ventricular filling before contraction, while Purkinje fibers ensure rapid, synchronous ventricular depolarization
choices.rationale: The slow AV nodal conduction (~0.05 m/s) allows atrial systole to finish filling ventricles before ventricular systole begins; Purkinje speed (~2-4 m/s) coordinates synchronous ventricular contraction to maximize ejection efficiency.

choices.rationale: AV delay increases end-diastolic volume by allowing complete atrial kick.

choices.rationale: Ejection occurs after AV nodal transmission, and Purkinje depolarization triggers AV valve closure, not opening.

explanation: The AV node introduces a physiological delay (~0.12 s) to ensure complete ventricular filling during atrial systole before ventricular contraction starts. In contrast, the Purkinje arborization conducts at ~2-4 m/s to depolarize all ventricular myocytes virtually simultaneously, creating a powerful, coordinated ejection wave from apex to base.
examTip: Slow AV conduction = optimal filling time ('atrial kick'); Fast Purkinje conduction = synchronous, coordinated ejection.

choices.text: A balance between inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels and outward K+ current
choices.rationale: Phase 2 (plateau) results from an electrical equilibrium where inward Ca2+ current via slow L-type calcium channels balances outward K+ efflux via delayed rectifier channels.

choices.text: Progressive closing of inward potassium rectifier channels without calcium entry

stem: At Point D (Phase 2 plateau) of the ventricular action potential diagram, what two opposing currents balance each other, and what is the key functional importance?

choices.text: Inward Na+ current balances outward K+ current; ensures rapid conduction across myocytes
choices.rationale: Fast Na+ channels are already inactivated during phase 2.

choices.text: Inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels balances outward K+ current; stimulates contraction and prolongs refractory period preventing tetanus
choices.rationale: At Point D (phase 2), inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels balances outward K+ current; this influx triggers excitation-contraction coupling and produces a prolonged refractory period that prevents cardiac tetanus.

choices.text: Outward Cl- current balances inward Ca2+ current; limits diastolic filling time
choices.rationale: Chloride current is not the primary balancing counter-ion in the cardiac plateau.

choices.text: Outward K+ current balances inward Cl- current; resets resting potential to -90 mV
choices.rationale: Point D is the plateau, not the final resting potential.

explanation: The sustained inward Ca2+ current during phase 2 serves two crucial physiological roles: it triggers calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) from the sarcoplasmic reticulum for muscular contraction, and it prolongs the refractory period, making summation and tetanus impossible in the heart.
examTip: Point D = Phase 2 plateau = Inward Ca2+ current (L-type) balances outward K+ current. Functional role = Contraction trigger + Tetanus prevention.

evidence.quote: What two opposing currents balance each other at point D, and what is the functional importance of this region? • At point D (phase 2, the plateau), inward Ca²⁺ current through L-type Ca²⁺ channels is balanced by outward K⁺ current. • The Ca²⁺ influx triggers further Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which stimulates contraction (excitation-contraction coupling). • The long plateau also prolongs the refractory period and prevents tetanus.
