explanation: Class I antiarrhythmic drugs (e.g. procainamide, lidocaine, flecainide) bind to fast voltage-gated Na+ channels, suppressing Phase 0 (Point B) and reducing the maximum rate of depolarizing upstroke (dV/dt max), thereby decreasing conduction velocity.
examTip: Fast sodium channel blockers (Class I antiarrhythmics) act directly on Point B (Phase 0 upstroke).

evidence.quote: If a drug blocked the fast sodium channels, which point would be most affected? • Point B would be most affected. • Blocking the fast Na⁺ channels slows and reduces the phase 0 upstroke, which lowers the conduction velocity. • Class I antiarrhythmic drugs act this way

stem: Which ionic event provides the essential trigger for calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (CICR) in ventricular myocytes?

choices.text: Sodium influx through funny channels during phase 4
choices.rationale: Funny channels are restricted to nodal pacemakers and do not trigger myocyte contraction.

choices.text: Calcium influx through L-type calcium channels during phase 2
choices.rationale: Inward Ca2+ flux through sarcolemmal L-type dihydropyridine receptors binds to and opens Ryanodine Receptors (RyR2) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, initiating calcium-induced calcium release.

choices.text: Potassium efflux through delayed rectifier channels in phase 3
choices.rationale: Potassium efflux repolarizes the membrane and promotes relaxation.

choices.text: Chloride entry through ligand-gated channels in phase 1
choices.rationale: Chloride flux does not trigger sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release.

explanation: Cardiac excitation-contraction coupling operates via Calcium-Induced Calcium Release (CICR): the small 'trigger' calcium entering via L-type channels during Phase 2 binds RyR2 receptors on the junctional SR, triggering massive release of stored Ca2+ into the cytosol to activate troponin C.
examTip: Trigger Ca2+ (L-type Ca2+ channel / DHPR) → opens RyR2 on SR → Massive Ca2+ release → Contraction.

evidence.quote: The Ca²⁺ influx triggers further Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which stimulates contraction (excitation-contraction coupling).

stem: Why is it physiologically impossible to tetanize normal cardiac ventricular muscle under physiological conditions?

choices.text: Cardiac muscle lacks sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium storage
choices.rationale: Cardiac muscle has an extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum network.

choices.text: The electrical refractory period lasts almost as long as the mechanical twitch
choices.rationale: Because the electrical absolute refractory period extends through phases 0, 1, 2, and mid-3 (lasting ~200-250 ms), the muscle has already begun relaxing before another action potential can be triggered, preventing summation and tetanus.

choices.text: Extracellular calcium concentrations are too low to sustain continuous contraction
choices.rationale: Extracellular calcium is ~2 mM, plenty to sustain contraction if channels remained open.

choices.text: Acetylcholine rapidly breaks down all intracellular troponin complexes
choices.rationale: Troponin is not degraded by acetylcholine.

explanation: In skeletal muscle, the action potential lasts only 1-2 ms, allowing repetitive high-frequency stimuli to produce wave summation and sustained tetanic contraction. In cardiac muscle, the long Phase 2 plateau creates an effective refractory period that spans nearly the entire mechanical twitch, ensuring the ventricles always relax and refill.
examTip: Cardiac muscle CANNOT be tetanized! Absolute refractory period overlaps mechanical contraction.

evidence.quote: The long plateau also prolongs the refractory period and prevents tetanus.

stem: Which electrophysiological property uniquely distinguishes the funny current (If) in the sinoatrial node from traditional voltage-gated sodium currents?

choices.text: It is activated by intense membrane depolarization above +20 mV
choices.rationale: Depolarization closes funny channels; they are activated by hyperpolarization.

choices.text: It is activated by membrane hyperpolarization at negative potentials (-50 to -65 mV)
choices.rationale: Funny (HCN) channels are uniquely opened by membrane hyperpolarization occurring at the termination of phase 3 repolarization, carrying inward sodium current to initiate spontaneous phase 4 prepotentials.

choices.text: It conducts exclusively potassium ions into the cell
choices.rationale: It is a non-selective cation channel carrying predominantly Na+ inward.

choices.text: It is completely insensitive to intracellular cyclic AMP levels
choices.rationale: HCN channels have cyclic nucleotide binding domains; cAMP shifts their activation curve to more positive potentials.

explanation: Funny channels (HCN4) earned their name because unlike almost all other voltage-gated channels that open upon depolarization, If channels open upon hyperpolarization at the end of repolarization, allowing Na+ to leak in and drive spontaneous diastolic depolarization.
examTip: HCN / Funny current: Activated by HYPERPOLARIZATION (not depolarization!) + Regulated by cAMP.

evidence.quote: Point B is phase 0, the rapid depolarization... autorhythmic impulses to control the heart

concept: Atrial Systole and Fourth Heart Sound Genesis
stem: During which stage of the cardiac cycle does active atrial contraction contribute the final ~10-20% of ventricular filling, potentially generating the fourth heart sound (S4)?

choices.rationale: Atrial systole is completed before isovolumetric contraction begins.
Atrial systole provides the 'atrial kick' assisting final ventricular filling; in stiff, non-compliant ventricles, this forceful inflow generates the abnormal fourth heart sound (S4).
Ventricles are contracting and ejecting blood into the aorta during rapid ejection.
Isovolumetric relaxation occurs in early diastole before AV valves open.

explanation: Atrial systole corresponds to the P wave on ECG. It tops off ventricular volume (End-Diastolic Volume ~120-130 mL). If ventricular compliance is reduced (e.g. hypertrophy), the blood rushing against the stiff wall produces S4.
examTip: S4 is an atrial gallop: 'Tennessee' (S4-S1-S2). It is ALWAYS diastolic and coincides with atrial contraction.

evidence.quote: 1 -> C. Atrial Systole Causes 4th heart sound & assists ventricular filling.

concept: Isovolumetric Contraction and First Heart Sound Genesis
stem: During which phase of the cardiac cycle are all four heart valves closed while ventricular pressure rises precipitously without changes in volume, marked by the first heart sound (S1)?

choices.rationale: AV valves are open during atrial systole.
Isovolumetric contraction begins with AV valve closure (producing S1); all valves remain closed while ventricular pressure spikes until exceeding arterial pressures.
Semilunar valves are wide open during rapid ejection.
Protodiastolic phase occurs at the end of systole just prior to semilunar valve closure.

explanation: Isovolumetric ventricular contraction represents the period between AV valve closure and semilunar valve opening. Ventricular tension builds enormously at fixed volume (closed chamber), generating S1 as the mitral and tricuspid valves snap shut.
examTip: Isovolumetric Contraction: All 4 valves CLOSED, Volume CONSTANT, Pressure RISING sharply, S1 heard.

evidence.quote: 2 -> F. Isovolumetric Contraction All valves closed; 1st heart sound upon AV closure.

stem: During which phase does intraventricular pressure reach its peak while semilunar valves are widely open and roughly two-thirds of the stroke volume is expelled?

choices.rationale: No ejection occurs during isovolumetric contraction because semilunar valves are closed.
During rapid ejection, semilunar valves are forced open, left ventricular pressure peaks (~120 mmHg), and ~70% of total stroke volume is rapidly propelled into the aorta.
During reduced ejection, ejection velocity slows down as pressure begins to fall.
No forward ejection occurs in the protodiastolic deceleration interval.

explanation: Rapid ventricular ejection accounts for the steepest drop in ventricular volume, the peak systolic blood pressure, and the maximum arterial blood flow velocity across the aortic and pulmonic valves.
examTip: Rapid ejection = Peak ventricular pressure + Maximal flow rate (~70% of SV expelled).

evidence.quote: 3 -> H. Rapid Ejection Maximum ventricular pressure; semilunar valves open.

stem: During which cardiac cycle phase does blood output into the great arteries decelerate as ventricular pressure begins to fall below peak arterial levels?

choices.rationale: Rapid ejection exhibits accelerating forward velocity and peak pressure.
In reduced ejection, myocardial repolarization (T wave) begins, ventricular contraction weakens, and blood outflow slows as momentum carries remaining stroke volume into the aorta.
The protodiastolic phase is the brief interval following the end of ejection.
All valves are closed during isovolumetric relaxation; no blood output occurs.

explanation: Reduced ejection corresponds to the T wave on the surface ECG. Ventricular pressure begins to decline below aortic pressure, yet forward flow briefly continues due to forward kinetic momentum.
examTip: Reduced ejection: Slower blood outflow, declining intraventricular pressure, corresponds to ECG T wave.

evidence.quote: 4 -> A. Reduced Ejection Slower blood output as pressure begins to drop.

stem: The shortest phase of the cardiac cycle, representing the brief ~0.04-second interval between the termination of ventricular systole and semilunar valve closure, is the:

choices.rationale: Rapid ejection lasts approximately 0.13 seconds.

The protodiastolic phase is the shortest phase (~0.04 s) of the cardiac cycle, occurring when ventricular contraction stops and pressure falls just enough for arterial backflow to close semilunar valves.
Isovolumetric relaxation lasts approximately 0.08 seconds.
Diastasis is the longest phase of the cycle (~0.20 seconds).

explanation: The protodiastolic phase is an extremely brief transition phase preceding semilunar valve closure. During this moment, ventricular contraction has ceased, and blood in the aorta reverses momentum toward the heart, catching the valve cusps.
examTip: Shortest phase = Protodiastolic phase (0.04 s). Longest phase = Diastasis / Reduced filling (0.20 s).

evidence.quote: 5 -> G. Protodiastolic Phase Shortest phase preceding semilunar valve closure.

concept: Isovolumetric Relaxation and Second Heart Sound Genesis
stem: During which cardiac cycle phase are all valves closed while ventricular pressure drops precipitously at constant volume, immediately preceded by the second heart sound (S2)?

choices.rationale: The semilunar valves close at the conclusion of protodiastole, initiating isovolumetric relaxation.
Isovolumetric relaxation begins with semilunar valve closure (producing S2); intraventricular pressure drops steeply from ~100 mmHg toward 0 mmHg without any volume change until AV valves open.
AV valves are open and volume increases rapidly during rapid filling.
Ventricular volume continues rising during reduced filling.

explanation: Isovolumetric relaxation represents the closed-chamber diastolic phase between semilunar valve closure (S2) and AV valve opening. Ventricular volume is at its absolute minimum (End-Systolic Volume ~50 mL) while pressure plunges.
examTip: Isovolumetric Relaxation: All valves CLOSED, Volume CONSTANT at minimum (ESV), Pressure DROPPING, S2 at onset.

evidence.quote: 6 -> B. Isovolumetric Relaxation All valves closed; rapid pressure drop; 2nd heart sound.

concept: Rapid Ventricular Filling and Third Heart Sound Genesis
stem: Which phase of the cardiac cycle begins immediately when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, allowing AV valves to open and producing a rush of blood that can generate a physiological third heart sound (S3)?

choices.rationale: AV valves remain closed throughout isovolumetric relaxation.
When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, AV valves open widely and blood accumulated in atria rushes in (~60-70% of filling); turbulence against ventricular walls can produce S3.
Filling slows down markedly during diastasis.
Atrial systole is late active filling, associated with S4.

explanation: Rapid ventricular filling occurs in early diastole. The vast majority of ventricular filling occurs passively during this phase. In young healthy individuals, children, or hyperdynamic states (pregnancy), the rapid inflow produces a benign S3.
examTip: S3 is a ventricular gallop: 'Kentucky' (S1-S2-S3). It occurs during early RAPID filling. Pathologic in older adults (heart failure / volume overload).

evidence.quote: 7 -> E. Rapid Filling Mitral valve opens; rapid flow causes 3rd heart sound.

stem: Which phase represents the longest period of ventricular diastole at resting heart rates, during which blood flows slowly from veins directly through atria into ventricles, with duration varying inversely with heart rate?

choices.rationale: Rapid filling is a relatively brief phase (~0.11 s) occurring before diastasis.
Diastasis is the longest cardiac cycle phase (~0.20 s at 75 bpm); filling slows down dramatically, and its duration is the most compromised when tachycardia shortens diastole.
Atrial systole is short (~0.10 s) and active.
Isovolumetric relaxation is brief (~0.08 s).

explanation: During diastasis (reduced filling), ventricular pressure approaches atrial pressure, and the rate of filling slows to a trickle. Because it is the longest phase, increases in heart rate primarily shorten diastasis without significantly compromising rapid filling.
examTip: Diastasis = Longest phase of cardiac cycle. When heart rate increases (tachycardia), diastasis duration is reduced the most.

evidence.quote: 8 -> D. Reduced Filling (Diastasis) Longest phase; duration varies inversely with heart rate.

stem: The first heart sound (S1) can be heard at the onset of which cardiac cycle phase?

choices.rationale: Atrial systole is associated with S4, not S1.
The first heart sound (S1) occurs at the beginning of isovolumetric ventricular contraction due to closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves.
Ventricular ejection follows isovolumetric contraction; no heart sound normally occurs during ejection.
Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation begins with the second heart sound (S2).

explanation: As ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure at the onset of ventricular systole, the AV valve leaflets are forced shut. The sudden deceleration of blood and vibration of valve leaflets, chordae tendineae, and ventricular walls produces S1.
examTip: S1 marks the beginning of ventricular systole (Isovolumetric Contraction); S2 marks the beginning of ventricular diastole (Isovolumetric Relaxation).

evidence.quote: The first heart sound can be heard at B. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction

stem: Which of the following mechanical events is directly associated with the production of the first heart sound?

choices.text: Rushing of blood into the ventricles due to atrial contraction
choices.rationale: Blood rushing into ventricles during atrial contraction generates S4.
The first heart sound (S1) is caused by closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves.
Closure of pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves causes the second heart sound (S2).
Valve opening is normally silent; opening snaps are pathological (e.g. mitral stenosis).

explanation: S1 represents the acoustic vibration caused by the closure of the mitral (M1) and tricuspid (T1) valves at the transition from diastole to systole, heard loudest at the apex.
examTip: S1 = Closure of AV valves (Mitral + Tricuspid). Normal valve opening is silent.

evidence.quote: Which of the following is associated with the first heart sound? B. Closing of the AV valves

stem: At the beginning of which phase of the cardiac cycle does the second heart sound occur?

choices.rationale: Atrial systole occurs in late diastole.
Isovolumetric contraction begins with S1.
S2 terminates ventricular ejection; it does not begin it.
The second heart sound (S2) occurs at the beginning of isovolumetric ventricular relaxation as semilunar valves close.

explanation: When ventricular pressure drops below aortic and pulmonary arterial pressures at the end of the protodiastolic phase, the semilunar valves snap shut, producing S2 and demarcating the beginning of isovolumetric relaxation.
examTip: Timing anchor: S1 = Start of Isovolumetric Contraction (systole). S2 = Start of Isovolumetric Relaxation (diastole).

evidence.quote: At beginning of which phase of cardiac cycle does the second heart sound occur? D. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation

stem: Which of the following mechanical events is associated with the second heart sound?

choices.rationale: The second heart sound (S2) consists of aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) semilunar valve closure.
Normal opening of AV valves is acoustically silent.

choices.text: Rushing of blood into the ventricles due to atrial contraction
choices.rationale: Atrial kick produces S4.

choices.text: Rapid flow of blood from the atria into the ventricles during ventricular filling
choices.rationale: Rapid passive ventricular filling can produce S3.

explanation: S2 is composed of two components: A2 (closure of the aortic valve) and P2 (closure of the pulmonary valve). A2 normally precedes P2, creating physiologic splitting during inspiration.
examTip: S2 = Closure of semilunar valves (Aortic A2 + Pulmonary P2).

evidence.quote: Which of the following is associated with the second heart sound? A. Closing of the pulmonary valves

stem: Which of the following mechanical events is associated with the generation of the third heart sound (S3)?

choices.text: Rushing of blood into the ventricles due to atrial contraction
choices.rationale: Atrial contraction rush generates S4, not S3.
Closing of pulmonary valves contributes P2 of S2.
Normal AV valve opening is silent.

choices.text: Rapid flow of blood from the atria into the ventricles during ventricular filling
choices.rationale: The third heart sound (S3) is caused by the rapid, turbulent inflow of blood from atria into ventricles during the early rapid filling phase.

explanation: S3 occurs in early diastole during passive rapid filling (~0.12-0.18 s after S2). Blood rushing into a compliant or volume-overloaded ventricle decelerates suddenly, setting up vibrations in the ventricular wall.
examTip: S3 = Early diastole, Rapid filling phase. Normal in youth/athletes; indicator of systolic heart failure / volume overload in adults.

evidence.quote: Which of the following is associated with the third heart sound? D. Rapid flow of blood from the atria into the ventricles during ventricular filling

stem: Which of the following mechanical events is associated with the generation of the fourth heart sound (S4)?

choices.text: Rushing of blood into the ventricles due to atrial contraction
choices.rationale: The fourth heart sound (S4) is caused by forceful atrial contraction propelling blood into a stiff or non-compliant ventricle in late diastole.
Pulmonary valve closure causes P2 of S2.
AV valve opening is silent.

choices.text: Rapid flow of blood from the atria into the ventricles during ventricular filling
choices.rationale: Early rapid passive filling produces S3.

explanation: S4 is an end-diastolic (presystolic) gallop sound produced when atrial contraction forces blood against a hypertrophied, non-compliant ventricular myocardium (e.g. chronic hypertension, aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy).
examTip: S4 = Late diastole, Atrial Systole ('atrial kick'). Always pathological; requires an active atrial contraction (cannot occur in atrial fibrillation!).

evidence.quote: Which of the following is associated with the fourth heart sound? A. Rushing of blood into the ventricles due to atrial contraction

stem: During which phase of the cardiac cycle is intraventricular blood volume at its lowest absolute level?

choices.rationale: Ventricular volume is at its maximum (EDV) at the end of atrial systole.
Ventricular volume is at EDV (~120 mL) during isovolumetric contraction.
Volume is progressively falling during ejection, but reaches its minimum at the end of ejection / isovolumetric relaxation.
Intraventricular volume is at its lowest level (End-Systolic Volume, ~50 mL) throughout isovolumetric ventricular relaxation.

explanation: Ventricles empty their stroke volume during ejection. The residual volume remaining in the ventricle—End-Systolic Volume (ESV, ~40-50 mL)—remains constant and at its absolute minimum throughout isovolumetric relaxation until the AV valves open.
examTip: Volume landmarks: Maximum volume (EDV) = Isovolumetric Contraction; Minimum volume (ESV) = Isovolumetric Relaxation.

evidence.quote: During which phase of the cardiac cycle is ventricular volume lowest? D. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation

stem: If heart rate increases markedly (tachycardia), which phase of the cardiac cycle is reduced by the greatest proportion?

choices.rationale: Atrial systole duration changes very little with rate.
Systolic contraction duration is relatively conserved.
Rapid filling is preserved to maintain viable hemodynamics.
Diastasis (reduced ventricular filling) is the longest diastolic phase and bears the overwhelming brunt of rate-dependent shortening.

explanation: As heart rate increases, total cardiac cycle duration decreases. Systole is relatively fixed, meaning diastole must shorten drastically. Within diastole, diastasis (reduced filling) is shortened first and most dramatically, eventually becoming virtually eliminated at extreme heart rates.
examTip: At high heart rates, DIASTOLE shortens much more than systole, and Diastasis (reduced filling) is compressed most.

evidence.quote: If heart rate increases, which phase of the cardiac cycle is decreased? D. Reduced ventricular filling

concept: Pressure Rise at Constant Volume Phase
stem: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does ventricular pressure rise steeply while ventricular volume remains strictly constant?

choices.rationale: Ventricular volume is actively increasing during atrial systole.
During isovolumetric ventricular contraction, all four cardiac valves are closed; myocyte tension generation causes pressure to skyrocket while volume remains unchanged.
Ventricular volume drops sharply during rapid ejection.
Ventricular volume continues to decline during reduced ejection.

explanation: By definition, 'isovolumetric' means constant volume. During isovolumetric contraction, the AV valves have closed but semilunar valves have not yet opened. Ventricular pressure rises from ~10 mmHg to 80 mmHg (aortic diastolic pressure) with zero change in chamber volume.
examTip: Key definition: Isovolumetric = Closed valves + Constant volume. If pressure is rising = Isovolumetric Contraction.

evidence.quote: During which phase of the cardiac cycle does ventricular pressure rise but ventricular volume remains constant? B. Isovolumetric ventricular contraction

concept: Longest Phase of the Cardiac Cycle
stem: The longest phase in the normal cardiac cycle at resting heart rate is the:

choices.rationale: Rapid ejection lasts only ~0.13 seconds.
Isovolumetric contraction lasts only ~0.05 seconds.
Rapid filling lasts only ~0.11 seconds.
Reduced ventricular filling (diastasis) is the longest individual phase (~0.20-0.22 seconds) of the 0.8-second normal cardiac cycle at 75 bpm.

explanation: At a resting heart rate of 75 bpm (total cycle = 0.8 s), systole occupies ~0.3 s and diastole ~0.5 s. The longest individual component phase is reduced ventricular filling (diastasis), lasting ~0.20 seconds.
examTip: Chronological extreme: Longest phase = Reduced ventricular filling / Diastasis (~0.20 s). Shortest phase = Protodiastolic phase (~0.04 s).

evidence.quote: The longest phase in cardiac cycle is D. Reduced ventricular filling phase

stem: All cardiac valves are closed simultaneously in which of the following phases of the cardiac cycle?

choices.rationale: During both isovolumetric phases (contraction and relaxation), all four heart valves (mitral, tricuspid, aortic, pulmonary) are closed simultaneously.
AV valves are open during atrial systole.
Semilunar valves are open during rapid ejection.
Semilunar valves are open during reduced ejection.

explanation: The heart operates as a closed chamber with all four valves shut during only two phases: isovolumetric contraction (rising pressure) and isovolumetric relaxation (falling pressure).
examTip: All 4 valves are CLOSED during: 1) Isovolumetric Contraction, and 2) Isovolumetric Relaxation.

evidence.quote: All cardiac valves are closed in A. Isovolumetric ventricular relaxation phase

concept: Ventricular Volume Behavior in Isovolumetric Contraction
stem: During the isovolumetric ventricular contraction, what happens to the ventricular volume?

choices.rationale: Volume only decreases when ejection begins.
Filling has already ended with AV valve closure.
Because both the AV valves and semilunar valves are completely closed and blood is an incompressible liquid, chamber volume remains strictly unchanged.

choices.text: Decreases as the ventricular pressure increases
choices.rationale: Pressure increases dramatically without any decrease in volume until the aortic valve opens.

explanation: Because myocardium contracts against an incompressible volume of trapped intracardiac blood in a sealed chamber, myocyte tension increases without macroscopic muscle shortening, keeping total ventricular volume strictly constant.
examTip: Isovolumetric contraction: Delta Volume = 0; Delta Pressure > 0 (sharp increase).

evidence.quote: During the isovolumetric ventricular contraction, what happens to the ventricular volume? C. Remains unchanged

stem: Which of the following happens during atrial systole of the cardiac cycle?

choices.rationale: S1 occurs after atrial systole, at the onset of isovolumetric contraction.
70-80% of filling occurs passively during the early rapid filling phase.
AV valves must be wide open for atrial blood to enter the ventricles.
During atrial systole (which occurs in ventricular diastole), the aortic semilunar valve is firmly closed to prevent regurgitation from the high-pressure aorta.

explanation: Atrial systole is the final phase of ventricular diastole. Throughout all diastolic phases, aortic pressure (~80-100 mmHg) far exceeds ventricular pressure (~5-10 mmHg), keeping the aortic valve tightly sealed.
examTip: During atrial systole: AV valves are OPEN; Semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves are CLOSED.

evidence.quote: Which of the following happens during atrial systole of the cardiac cycle? D. The aortic valve is closed

stem: AV valves are open during which of the following phases of the cardiac cycle?

choices.rationale: AV valves close at the start of isovolumetric contraction.
AV valves are open throughout ventricular filling, including rapid filling, reduced filling, and atrial systole.
AV valves are still closed during protodiastole as ventricular pressure is still above atrial pressure.
AV valves are closed throughout ejection to prevent regurgitation into atria.

explanation: Atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves are open whenever ventricular pressure is lower than atrial pressure, which encompasses rapid filling, diastasis, and atrial systole.
examTip: AV valves are OPEN during ventricular DIASTOLE (filling phases + atrial systole).

evidence.quote: AV valves are open during which of the following phases of cardiac cycle? B. Atrial systole

concept: Ventricular vs Atrial Pressure Gradient Comparison
stem: Ventricular pressure is higher than the atrial pressure in all following phases of cardiac cycle EXCEPT

choices.rationale: Ventricular pressure is higher than atrial pressure, holding the AV valves shut.
During atrial systole, atrial pressure is higher than ventricular pressure, driving blood forward across open AV valves into the ventricles.
Ventricular pressure is enormously higher (~120 mmHg) than atrial pressure (~5-10 mmHg).
Ventricular pressure remains substantially higher than atrial pressure throughout ejection.

explanation: During atrial systole, the contracting atrium generates a small pressure gradient (~2-5 mmHg) exceeding intraventricular pressure, which keeps the AV valve open and drives the final burst of ventricular inflow.
examTip: Whenever Ventricular Pressure > Atrial Pressure: AV valves are CLOSED (Systole). Whenever Atrial Pressure > Ventricular Pressure: AV valves are OPEN (Diastole).

evidence.quote: Ventricular pressure is higher than the atrial pressure in all following phases of cardiac cycle EXCEPT B. Atrial systole

stem: All of the following phases are involved in ventricular filling EXCEPT

choices.rationale: Atrial systole provides ~10-20% of ventricular filling.
Rapid ventricular ejection is a phase of ventricular systole that EMPTIES the ventricles, rather than filling them.
Rapid filling provides ~60-70% of ventricular filling.
Reduced filling provides ~10% of ventricular filling.

explanation: Ventricular filling comprises three distinct diastolic phases: rapid ventricular filling (early diastole), reduced ventricular filling/diastasis (mid-diastole), and atrial systole (late diastole). Rapid ejection empties the ventricles.
examTip: Ventricular Filling = 1) Rapid filling, 2) Reduced filling (diastasis), 3) Atrial systole. Ejection is EMPTYING.

evidence.quote: All are involved in ventricular filing EXCEPT B. Rapid ventricular ejection

stem: All cardiac valves (AV and semilunar) are opened simultaneously in which phase of the cardiac cycle?

choices.rationale: All valves are CLOSED in isovolumetric relaxation.
All valves are CLOSED in isovolumetric contraction.
In both isovolumetric phases, all valves are closed, not open.
Under normal physiological conditions, there is NO phase of the cardiac cycle in which all four cardiac valves are open at the same time.

explanation: Because ventricular pressure cannot be simultaneously higher than arterial pressure and lower than atrial pressure, the AV valves and semilunar valves never open concurrently. Thus, all four valves are NEVER open at the same time.
examTip: Valvular rule: All 4 valves can be CLOSED at once (Isovolumetric phases), but all 4 are NEVER OPEN at once!

evidence.quote: All cardiac valves are opened in D. None of the above

stem: In ventricular filling phase, which of the following is true?

choices.rationale: Atrial contraction contributes only ~10-20% of total filling; the majority is passive.
Filling cannot begin during isovolumetric relaxation because AV valves remain closed.

choices.text: Gives rise to third heart sound
choices.rationale: Rapid passive inflow of blood during early ventricular filling causes turbulence against ventricular walls that can produce the third heart sound (S3).
Ventricular filling is predominantly passive diastole, driven by venous return rather than active ventricular ATP consumption.

explanation: During early rapid ventricular filling, blood rushes through open AV valves. The sudden deceleration of this fluid column within the expanding ventricle generates the third heart sound (S3).
examTip: Third heart sound (S3) = Early rapid passive filling. Fourth heart sound (S4) = Late active filling (atrial systole).

evidence.quote: In ventricular filling phase, it C. Gives rise to third heart sound

concept: Ventricular Emptying Fraction during Rapid Ejection
stem: Roughly 70% of the total ventricular emptying occurs in which phase of the cardiac cycle?

choices.rationale: No forward ejection occurs in protodiastole.
All valves are closed; no emptying occurs.
Approximately two-thirds (~70%) of total stroke volume is rapidly expelled during the first third of ventricular systole (rapid ejection phase).
The remaining ~30% of stroke volume is slowly ejected during reduced ejection.

explanation: Ventricular ejection is distinctly biphasic: rapid ejection accounts for the initial 70% of stroke volume expelled under high pressure, while reduced ejection accounts for the remaining 30% as intraventricular pressure begins to fall.
examTip: Ejection fraction distribution: ~70% ejected during Rapid Ejection; ~30% ejected during Reduced Ejection.

evidence.quote: 70% of the ventricular emptying occurs in C. Rapid ventricular ejection

concept: Protodiastolic Phase Valve States and Pressure Gradients
stem: During the protodiastolic phase of the cardiac cycle, which precise combination of valve states and pressure gradients occurs immediately following the end of ventricular systole?

choices.text: Aortic and pulmonary valves are closing while ventricular pressure falls below the pressure inside the aorta
choices.rationale: In protodiastole, ventricular contraction ceases, ventricular pressure drops below aortic/pulmonary pressure, and reverse momentum of blood begins closing the semilunar valves.

choices.text: Atrioventricular valves open simultaneously while ventricular volume increases rapidly due to early venous return
choices.rationale: AV valves remain closed; they do not open until after isovolumetric relaxation.

choices.text: Semilunar valves remain fully open while ventricular pressure exceeds both atrial and arterial pressure gradients
choices.rationale: Ventricular pressure has already fallen below arterial pressure.

choices.text: All four cardiac valves remain completely closed as ventricular pressure rises sharply while volume stays constant
choices.rationale: This describes isovolumetric contraction, not protodiastole.

explanation: The protodiastolic phase marks the brief hemodynamic transition where myocyte relaxation begins, ventricular pressure dips below aortic and pulmonary pressures, and the back-eddy of arterial blood catches the semilunar valve cusps, closing them.
examTip: Protodiastole = Semilunar valves closing as ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure.

evidence.quote: During the protodiastolic phase of the cardiac cycle, which precise combination of valve states and pressure gradients occurs immediately following the end of ventricular systole? 1. Aortic and pulmonary valves are closing while ventricular pressure falls below the pressure inside the aorta

concept: Tachycardia Impact on Diastasis and Stroke Volume
stem: According to the properties of reduced ventricular filling (diastasis) and heart rate variations, what occurs when a person's heart rate increases significantly?

choices.text: The duration of diastasis lengthens proportionally, allowing a higher end-diastolic filling volume
choices.rationale: Tachycardia markedly shortens diastasis; it does not lengthen it.

choices.text: The filling time is shortened, leading to decreased end-diastolic volume and lower stroke volume
choices.rationale: Excessive tachycardia markedly shortens ventricular diastolic filling time, reducing end-diastolic volume (EDV) and consequently decreasing stroke volume according to Frank-Starling law.

choices.text: Atrial systole becomes the primary contributor, accounting for 80% of total active ventricular filling
choices.rationale: Atrial systole cannot compensate to provide 80% of total filling.

choices.text: The protodiastolic phase is completely eliminated from the cardiac cycle to preserve myocardial output
choices.rationale: Protodiastole is not eliminated.

explanation: When heart rate exceeds physiological limits (e.g. severe tachyarrhythmias > 160-180 bpm), diastole is compressed so severely that even rapid filling is compromised. End-diastolic volume plummets, causing stroke volume and cardiac output to fall dangerously.
examTip: High heart rate → Shortened diastole → ↓ Filling time → ↓ EDV → ↓ Stroke Volume (Frank-Starling law).

evidence.quote: According to the properties of reduced ventricular filling (diastasis) and heart rate variations, what occurs when a person's heart rate increases significantly? 2. The filling time is shortened, leading to decreased end-diastolic volume and lower stroke volume

stem: Arterial blood pressure is best defined as

choices.text: Force exerted by blood on venous walls
choices.rationale: Venous pressure represents the force in the venous system, not arterial pressure.

choices.text: Lateral force of blood on arterial walls
choices.rationale: Arterial blood pressure is physiologically defined as the lateral force exerted by the column of blood against the unit area of the arterial vessel wall.
Longitudinal force propels blood flow downstream; pressure is specifically the lateral distending force.
Arterial pressure persists throughout diastole due to elastic recoil of the aorta.

explanation: Hydrodynamically, blood pressure is the lateral (radial) force exerted per unit area of vessel wall. In clinical practice, although longitudinal pressure gradients drive forward laminar flow, the pressure recorded by sphygmomanometry is lateral wall tension.
examTip: Blood pressure is LATERAL force against arterial walls. Diastolic pressure is maintained by aortic elastic recoil (Windkessel effect).

evidence.quote: Arterial blood pressure is best defined as... Longitudinal force along blood vessels / Lateral force of blood on arterial walls

concept: Primary Determinants of Arterial Blood Pressure
stem: Arterial blood pressure is determined primarily by which of the following physiological factors?

choices.rationale: Heart rate and stroke volume determine cardiac output, which is only one component of BP.
Blood volume and viscosity influence preload and resistance but are not the primary hemodynamic formula components.
Mean arterial pressure is fundamentally determined by the product of cardiac output and total peripheral resistance (MAP = CO × TPR).
Preload regulates stroke volume via Frank-Starling, but systemic pressure requires peripheral resistance.

explanation: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) is governed by Ohm's law analog for hemodynamics: ΔP = Flow × Resistance, meaning MAP ≈ Cardiac Output (CO) × Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR).
examTip: Hemodynamic cardinal equation: Blood Pressure = Cardiac Output (CO) × Total Peripheral Resistance (TPR).

evidence.quote: Arterial blood pressure is determined primarily by C. Cardiac output and resistance

stem: Cardiac output is defined as

choices.rationale: Volume ejected per single heartbeat is the stroke volume (~70 mL).
Cardiac output is defined as the volume of blood pumped by each ventricle per unit time, conventionally expressed as liters per minute (L/min).
Pressure developed per beat reflects systolic ventricular pressure.
Arteriolar resistance is total peripheral resistance.

explanation: Cardiac output (CO) is the product of heart rate (HR) and stroke volume (SV): CO = HR × SV. In a healthy resting 70-kg adult, CO is approximately 72 bpm × 70 mL = ~5.0 L/min.
examTip: Cardiac Output (CO) = Volume pumped per minute (L/min) = Heart Rate (HR) × Stroke Volume (SV).

evidence.quote: Cardiac output is defined as B. Blood pumped per minute

concept: Main Site of Total Peripheral Resistance
stem: Total peripheral resistance mainly reflects resistance generated in the:

choices.rationale: Large arteries have wide diameters and negligible resistance; they function as conduits and capacitors.
Arterioles are the primary resistance vessels (stopcocks of the circulation) possessing rich vascular smooth muscle and high tone.
Veins are low-resistance capacitance vessels.
The pulmonary bed is a low-resistance circuit (TPR is ~10-fold higher in systemic arterioles).

explanation: By Poiseuille's law (Resistance ∝ 1/r^4), small changes in the internal radius of highly muscular arterioles produce dramatic shifts in resistance, establishing arterioles as the chief site of systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure regulation.
examTip: Resistance vessels = Arterioles (greatest drop in mean pressure, regulate TPR). Capacitance vessels = Veins.

evidence.quote: Total peripheral resistance mainly reflects resistance in B. Systemic arterioles

stem: Systolic blood pressure occurs during which cardiac mechanical phase?

choices.rationale: Diastolic blood pressure occurs during ventricular relaxation.
Atrial contraction occurs in late ventricular diastole.
Systolic blood pressure represents the peak pressure reached in the systemic arteries during ventricular contraction (systole).
Aortic pressure is declining toward diastolic levels during isovolumetric relaxation.

explanation: Systolic blood pressure (normal ~120 mmHg) is generated when the contracting left ventricle ejects blood into the aorta faster than it can run off through peripheral arterioles, distending the aortic wall.
examTip: Systolic BP = Peak arterial pressure during ventricular contraction. Diastolic BP = Lowest arterial pressure during ventricular relaxation.

evidence.quote: Systolic blood pressure occurs during C. Ventricular contraction

stem: Pulse pressure represents the difference between

choices.rationale: Mean arterial pressure minus diastolic pressure equals approximately one-third of pulse pressure.
Pulse pressure is mathematically defined as systolic blood pressure minus diastolic blood pressure (PP = SBP − DBP).
This reflects the systemic driving pressure gradient.
This reflects the atrioventricular pressure gradient.

explanation: Pulse pressure (normally ~40 mmHg, e.g. 120 − 80 mmHg) is directly proportional to stroke volume and inversely proportional to arterial compliance. Stiff, atherosclerotic arteries produce a wide pulse pressure.
examTip: Pulse Pressure = Systolic Pressure − Diastolic Pressure. Proportional to Stroke Volume; inversely proportional to arterial compliance.

evidence.quote: Pulse pressure represents the difference between B. Systolic and diastolic pressure

concept: Baroreceptor Reflex Compensatory Response to Hypotension
stem: When arterial blood pressure falls acutely, which combination of cardiovascular compensatory responses is triggered by the baroreceptor reflex?

choices.text: Venodilation, decreased contractility, bradycardia, arteriolar dilation
choices.rationale: These parasympathetic-dominated responses would worsen hypotension.

choices.text: Venoconstriction, increased contractility, increased heart rate, arteriolar vasoconstriction
choices.rationale: Baroreceptor disinhibition disinhibits the sympathetic vasomotor center, producing venoconstriction (↑ venous return), ↑ contractility (↑ stroke volume), ↑ heart rate, and arteriolar vasoconstriction (↑ TPR).

choices.text: Selective renal vasodilation, vagal stimulation, reduced venous return
choices.rationale: Vagal stimulation reduces heart rate and BP.

choices.text: Inhibition of sympathetic ganglia with increased urinary sodium excretion
choices.rationale: Sympathetic activation stimulates renin release and sodium retention.

explanation: A decrease in arterial blood pressure decreases stretch on carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors, reducing afferent firing to the NTS. The medullary vasomotor center responds by increasing sympathetic adrenergic outflow to veins (venoconstriction), heart (↑ HR and contractility), and arterioles (vasoconstriction).
examTip: Baroreceptor response to low BP: ↑ Heart rate, ↑ Contractility, ↑ Arteriolar vasoconstriction (TPR), ↑ Venoconstriction (venous return).

evidence.quote: Mention the effects of baroreceptor reflex in attempt to increase the arterial pressure towards the normal: 1. Vasoconstriction of veins 2. ↑ Contractility 3. ↑ Heart rate 4. Vasoconstriction of arterioles

stem: The baroreceptor reflex is classified physiologically as a:

choices.rationale: Long-term pressure regulation is renal and hormonal (RAAS), operating over hours to days.
Renal mechanisms modulate extracellular fluid volume.
Baroreceptors operate via neural autonomic reflex arcs.
The baroreceptor reflex is a rapid, short-term neural feedback mechanism that acts within seconds to buffer beat-to-beat blood pressure fluctuations.

explanation: Neural reflexes (baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflexes) respond in seconds to correct acute changes in arterial blood pressure (e.g. postural transitions from lying to standing), but they reset to higher pressures in chronic hypertension.
examTip: Short-term BP control = Neural baroreceptors (seconds). Long-term BP control = Renal-endocrine RAAS / blood volume (hours/days).

evidence.quote: The baroreceptor reflex is classified as D. Rapid short-term mechanism

stem: High-pressure baroreceptors involved in systemic blood pressure regulation are located mainly in the:

choices.rationale: Kidneys have juxtaglomerular apparatus baroreceptors regulating renin, but neural baroreflex sensors are in carotid and aortic walls.
The primary arterial baroreceptors are spray-type nerve endings embedded in the adventitia/media of the carotid sinus (bifurcation of common carotid) and aortic arch.
Coronary vessels do not house the primary arterial baroreceptor reflex afferents.
Atrial stretch receptors are low-pressure cardiopulmonary receptors, not systemic arterial baroreceptors.

explanation: Carotid sinus baroreceptors transmit sensory afferents via the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX, Hering's nerve), whereas aortic arch baroreceptors transmit afferents via the vagus nerve (CN X).
examTip: Baroreceptor anatomy: Carotid Sinus = CN IX (Glossopharyngeal); Aortic Arch = CN X (Vagus).

evidence.quote: Baroreceptors involved in blood pressure regulation are located mainly in B. Carotid sinus and aortic arch

concept: Baroreceptor Firing Rate Response to Hypertension
stem: An acute increase in arterial blood pressure causes arterial baroreceptors to

choices.rationale: Increased arterial pressure distends the vascular walls, opening stretch-sensitive mechanosensitive ion channels and increasing afferent nerve action potential firing rate.
Decreased firing rate occurs when arterial blood pressure falls.
Baroreceptors fire tonic baselines and increase firing with higher pressure.
Baroreceptors are sensory afferents projecting to the brainstem nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS).

explanation: The firing rate of baroreceptors is directly proportional to both the absolute mean arterial pressure and the rate of pressure change (dP/dt). High pressure stretches the wall, increasing afferent firing to the NTS.
examTip: ↑ Blood pressure → ↑ Arterial wall stretch → ↑ Baroreceptor afferent firing rate.

evidence.quote: An increase in arterial blood pressure causes baroreceptors to A. Increase firing rate

stem: Increased baroreceptor afferent firing to the medullary cardiovascular center results in

choices.rationale: Increased baroreceptor firing inhibits the rostral ventrolateral medulla (sympathetic center).
Parasympathetic vagal outflow is increased, not decreased.
Increased afferent firing excites the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus, enhancing efferent vagal parasympathetic output to slow heart rate and reduce BP.
Vasoconstrictor center inhibition leads to vasodilation.

explanation: When high BP increases baroreceptor discharge to the NTS, the NTS excites parasympathetic nuclei (increasing vagal tone to the SA node) and inhibits the sympathetic vasomotor center, producing bradycardia and vasodilation.
examTip: High BP reflex: ↑ Baroreceptor firing → ↑ Vagal parasympathetic output (bradycardia) + ↓ Sympathetic tone (vasodilation) → BP returns to normal.

evidence.quote: Increased baroreceptor firing results in C. Increased vagal activity

stem: A sudden fall in arterial blood pressure leads to which autonomic efferent response?

choices.rationale: Parasympathetic vagal output is inhibited to permit tachycardia.
Sympathetic outflow is strongly activated.
Decreased baroreceptor stretch disinhibits the sympathetic vasomotor area, unleashing increased sympathetic adrenergic activation to restore BP.
Arteriolar vasoconstriction occurs to elevate total peripheral resistance.

explanation: When mean arterial pressure drops (e.g. orthostatic pooling or hemorrhage), reduced afferent input relieves NTS inhibition of the sympathetic presympathetic neurons in the RVLM, driving intense sympathetic discharge.
examTip: Low BP reflex: ↓ Baroreceptor firing → ↓ Vagal activity + ↑ Sympathetic activation (tachycardia + vasoconstriction).

evidence.quote: A fall in arterial blood pressure leads to C. Increased sympathetic activation

stem: During acute hypovolemic hemorrhage, heart rate increases reflexively mainly due to

choices.rationale: Vagal discharge slows heart rate; it is withdrawn in hemorrhage.
Arterial stretch is reduced due to hypovolemia.
Parasympathetic tone is depressed.
Hemorrhage reduces circulating blood volume and arterial pressure, reducing baroreceptor stretch and firing, which disinhibits sympathetic outflow and causes reflex tachycardia.

explanation: Acute blood loss drops venous return, end-diastolic volume, stroke volume, and arterial blood pressure. Carotid and aortic baroreceptor stretch decreases, reducing afferent firing and releasing the sympathetic accelerator to produce tachycardia.
examTip: Hemorrhage: ↓ Blood volume → ↓ Arterial pressure → ↓ Baroreceptor firing → ↑ Sympathetic tone → Reflex Tachycardia.

evidence.quote: During hemorrhage, heart rate increases mainly due to D. Reduced baroreceptor firing

concept: Arteriolar Response to Sympathetic Adrenergic Stimulation
stem: Sympathetic adrenergic stimulation of systemic arterioles causes

choices.rationale: Norepinephrine released from sympathetic postganglionic fibers binds to alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on vascular smooth muscle, causing vasoconstriction and increasing total peripheral resistance.
Alpha-1 mediated vasoconstriction elevates resistance and blood pressure.
Peripheral resistance increases.
Arteriolar smooth muscle is densely innervated by sympathetic fibers and highly responsive.

explanation: Sympathetic postganglionic varicosities release norepinephrine, which activates Gq-coupled alpha-1 adrenergic receptors on arteriolar vascular smooth muscle cells, triggering IP3-mediated intracellular calcium release and potent vasoconstriction.
examTip: Arteriolar sympathetic stimulation: Norepinephrine + Alpha-1 receptor → Vasoconstriction → ↑ TPR → ↑ Blood Pressure.

evidence.quote: Sympathetic stimulation of arterioles causes A. Vasoconstriction and increased resistance

stem: Venoconstriction triggered during acute hemorrhage results in which beneficial hemodynamic outcome?

choices.rationale: Unstressed volume is decreased as blood is mobilized into stressed volume.
Venous return is enhanced to preserve cardiac filling.
Sympathetic alpha-1 constriction of venous capacitance vessels increases effective circulating blood volume and mean systemic filling pressure, augmenting venous return to the heart.
Mean systemic filling pressure is increased.

explanation: Veins contain ~70% of total blood volume (capacitance reservoir / unstressed volume). Sympathetic venoconstriction compresses this reservoir, shifting unstressed volume into stressed volume, increasing central venous pressure and restoring venous return.
examTip: Venoconstriction = Capacitance mobilization: Shifts unstressed to stressed volume → ↑ Mean systemic filling pressure → ↑ Venous return.

evidence.quote: Venoconstriction during hemorrhage results in C. Increased venous return

stem: Which of the following summarizes the coordinated physiological actions of Angiotensin II to restore arterial blood pressure to normal?

choices.text: Inhibits aldosterone, promotes natriuresis, decreases thirst, and causes systemic vasodilation
choices.rationale: These are actions of ANP, not Angiotensin II.

choices.text: Stimulates aldosterone secretion, directly increases renal Na+ reabsorption, stimulates thirst, and causes arteriolar vasoconstriction
choices.rationale: Angiotensin II restores blood pressure by: 1) Stimulating adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, 2) Directly enhancing tubular Na+ reabsorption, 3) Stimulating hypothalamic thirst/drinking, and 4) Causing potent arteriolar vasoconstriction.

choices.text: Suppresses sympathetic vasomotor centers and promotes potassium retention by renal collecting ducts
choices.rationale: Angiotensin II enhances sympathetic activity and promotes potassium excretion via aldosterone.

choices.text: Induces bradycardia and relaxes vascular smooth muscle via nitric oxide release
choices.rationale: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and pressor agent.

explanation: Angiotensin II acts via AT1 Gq-protein coupled receptors across multiple organ systems: it constricts arterioles to elevate TPR, stimulates zona glomerulosa cells to secrete aldosterone, upregulates apical Na+/H+ exchangers in the proximal tubule, and stimulates the hypothalamic thirst center and ADH release.
examTip: Angiotensin II four key actions: 1) Vasoconstriction (↑ TPR), 2) Aldosterone release (Na+/H2O retention), 3) Thirst stimulation, 4) Direct renal Na+ reabsorption.

evidence.quote: Mention the effects of angiotensin II in attempt to increase the arterial pressure towards the normal: 1. It stimulates secretion of aldosterone by the adrenal cortex. 2. It directly increases Na+ reabsorption. 3. It increases thirst. 4. It causes vasoconstriction of the arterioles

stem: The long-term physiological mechanism for the regulation of arterial blood pressure involves regulating which of the following parameters?

choices.rationale: Vessel diameter adjustments provide rapid short-term neural control.
Long-term arterial blood pressure control is governed primarily by the kidneys adjusting extracellular fluid and blood volume via pressure natriuresis and hormonal systems (RAAS, ADH).
Myocardial contractility modulations provide acute beat-to-beat hemodynamic regulation.
Heart rate changes are mediated by fast neural reflexes.

explanation: Guyton's renal-body fluid feedback mechanism establishes that chronic, long-term blood pressure control is fundamentally tied to kidney regulation of extracellular fluid volume (blood volume). As long as kidneys maintain fluid balance, long-term blood pressure remains stable.
examTip: Short-term BP regulation = Neural (baroreceptors, vessel diameter, HR). Long-term BP regulation = Renal (blood volume, extracellular fluid).

evidence.quote: The long-term mechanism for regulation of arterial blood pressure involves regulating which of the following? B. Blood volume

stem: What specialized cells in the kidney monitor renal perfusion pressure and release renin when arterial pressure is low?

choices.rationale: Cortical tubular epithelial cells do not synthesize renin.
Angiotensinogen is produced and secreted continuously by hepatocytes in the liver.
Aldosterone is synthesized in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex.

Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells in the afferent arterioles of the renal glomeruli synthesize, store, and release renin in response to decreased renal perfusion pressure, sympathetic beta-1 tone, or reduced NaCl delivery to the macula densa.

explanation: Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells are modified vascular smooth muscle cells situated predominantly in the wall of the afferent arteriole. They act as intrarenal baroreceptors: when perfusion pressure falls, stretch decreases, triggering exocytosis of renin granules.
examTip: Renin source = Juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of renal afferent arteriole. Stimulated by: ↓ Renal perfusion pressure, ↓ NaCl at macula densa, ↑ Sympathetic beta-1 drive.

evidence.quote: What cells in the kidney monitor blood pressure, releasing renin when renal perfusion pressure is low? D. Juxtaglomerular cell

stem: The angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE)

choices.text: Is normally absent in the plasma
choices.rationale: ACE is present on pulmonary vascular endothelium and circulating in plasma.
Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction; ACE is the catalytic enzyme producing it.

choices.text: It converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II
choices.rationale: Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE), located predominantly on the luminal surface of pulmonary capillary endothelial cells, cleaves two amino acids from the decapeptide Angiotensin I to form the active octapeptide Angiotensin II.

choices.text: It converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I
choices.rationale: Renin converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

explanation: Renin from the kidney cleaves liver-derived circulating angiotensinogen into the decapeptide angiotensin I. As angiotensin I circulates through the pulmonary microvasculature, endothelial-bound ACE (kininase II) converts it into the bioactive octapeptide angiotensin II (and simultaneously degrades bradykinin).
examTip: Renin: Angiotensinogen → Angiotensin I. ACE: Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II (also degrades bradykinin, explaining ACE-inhibitor cough).

evidence.quote: The angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) C. It converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II

stem: Angiotensin II contributes to blood pressure elevation through which of the following central nervous system mechanisms?

choices.text: Is formed by the action of an enzyme on angiotensin III
choices.rationale: Angiotensin II is formed from Angiotensin I, and Angiotensin III is a degradation metabolite of Angiotensin II.

choices.text: Is released from the atrial musculature
choices.rationale: ANP is released from atrial musculature; Angiotensin II is produced enzymatically in the vascular lumen.

choices.text: Acts through stimulating the vasomotor center
choices.rationale: Circulating Angiotensin II crosses fenestrated circumventricular organs (e.g. area postrema, subfornical organ) to stimulate central sympathetic vasomotor centers and increase systemic sympathetic outflow.

choices.text: Is formed due to presence of renin in the circulation
choices.rationale: Renin forms Angiotensin I; ACE forms Angiotensin II directly.

explanation: Besides direct peripheral vasoconstriction, Angiotensin II acts centrally at circumventricular brain regions lacking a blood-brain barrier to stimulate the medullary vasomotor center, enhancing sympathetic tone and stimulating thirst and vasopressin release.
examTip: Angiotensin II central pressor effect: Acts on circumventricular organs → Stimulates medullary vasomotor center → ↑ Central sympathetic outflow.

evidence.quote: Angiotensin II C. Acts through stimulating the vasomotor center

stem: The overall physiological action of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) on the cardiovascular system includes

choices.rationale: Erythropoietin (EPO), not RAAS, primarily stimulates erythropoiesis.
RAAS does not decrease myocardial contractility.
RAAS causes vasoconstriction, which decreases vessel radius.

Through aldosterone-mediated renal sodium/water reabsorption and ADH-mediated water retention, the net systemic effect of RAAS activation is an increase in extracellular fluid and total circulating blood volume.

explanation: Activation of the RAAS cascade results in systemic vasoconstriction and renal sodium and water conservation, expanding intravascular plasma volume and raising blood pressure back toward the homeostatic set point.
examTip: RAAS ultimate objective: Restore arterial blood pressure and organ perfusion by ↑ Systemic vascular resistance + ↑ Extracellular Blood Volume.

evidence.quote: The action of renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system includes D. Increase in blood volume

stem: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS)?

choices.text: Adrenal cortex plays a role in its actions
choices.rationale: True: the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex releases aldosterone in response to Angiotensin II.

This is FALSE (the correct answer): RAAS is an intermediate-to-long-term hormonal cascade requiring minutes to hours for enzymatic cleavage and hours to days for aldosterone transcriptional changes, unlike rapid neural baroreflexes.

choices.text: It acts by controlling blood volume
choices.rationale: True: RAAS modulates blood volume via renal sodium handling.
True: RAAS utilizes peptide hormones (Ang II) and steroid hormones (aldosterone).

explanation: Neural baroreceptor reflexes respond in seconds, whereas hormonal systems like RAAS act over an intermediate-to-long timescale. Aldosterone requires hours to stimulate gene transcription of ENaC and Na+/K+ ATPase pumps in renal principal cells.
examTip: Response speeds: Neural baroreceptors = seconds (rapid); Renin-Angiotensin = minutes to hours; Aldosterone = hours to days (slow gene expression).

evidence.quote: Which of the following is false about renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system? B. It is rapid

concept: Renin-Angiotensin System Substrate and Synthesis Source
stem: All of the following statements regarding the renin-angiotensin system are correct EXCEPT

choices.rationale: Hypovolemia and hemorrhage are classic powerful triggers for renin release.

choices.text: Depends on angiotensinogen secretion from the juxtaglomerular apparatus
choices.rationale: This is FALSE (the correct answer for EXCEPT): Angiotensinogen is synthesized and secreted by the LIVER (hepatocytes), not the renal juxtaglomerular apparatus; the JG apparatus secretes renin.

choices.text: Promotes aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex
choices.rationale: Angiotensin II directly stimulates adrenal aldosterone synthesis.
Angiotensin II is one of the most potent known endogenous vasoconstrictors.

explanation: Angiotensinogen is a large circulating alpha-2 globulin produced continuously by the liver. Juxtaglomerular cells in the kidney produce the proteolytic enzyme renin, not angiotensinogen.
examTip: Key organ origins: Angiotensinogen = Liver; Renin = Kidneys (JG cells); ACE = Lungs (endothelium); Aldosterone = Adrenal cortex.

evidence.quote: All about renin-angiotensin system is correct, EXCEPT B. Depends on angiotensinogen secretion from the juxtaglomerular apparatus

stem: Which of the following would be expected to occur in response to unilateral constriction (stenosis) of the renal artery?

choices.rationale: Renal hypoperfusion activates RAAS, which reduces urinary sodium excretion to expand volume.
Secondary renovascular hypertension develops, significantly elevating systemic arterial pressure.
Renin release is markedly stimulated by the hypoperfused post-stenotic kidney.
Constriction of the renal artery drops perfusion pressure to the ipsilateral kidney, triggering massive juxtaglomerular renin release and a consequent elevation in circulating Angiotensin II levels.

explanation: Renal artery stenosis triggers the classic Goldblatt mechanism: the kidney senses falsely low systemic pressure, releasing excess renin that converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, driving up Angiotensin II and aldosterone, resulting in renovascular hypertension.
examTip: Renal artery stenosis → Post-stenotic hypotension → Massive JG Renin secretion → ↑ Angiotensin II & Aldosterone → Renovascular Hypertension.

evidence.quote: Which of the following would be expected to occur in response to constriction of the renal artery? D. Increase angiotensin II

stem: A patient presents with pathologically elevated secretion of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH / Vasopressin, e.g. SIADH). Which of the following arterial blood pressure readings would be most consistent with the biological actions of high ADH?

choices.rationale: This represents hypotension, inconsistent with the water-retentive and vasopressor effects of excess ADH.
This represents completely normal blood pressure.
This exhibits a widened pulse pressure, uncharacteristic of vasopressin-induced vasoconstriction.

Excessive ADH causes marked water retention via renal V2 receptors (expanding intravascular volume) and potent arteriolar vasoconstriction via vascular V1 receptors, producing marked arterial hypertension.

explanation: Antidiuretic hormone acts via two major receptor classes: renal V2 receptors in collecting ducts to insert aquaporin-2 water channels (increasing water reabsorption and blood volume), and vascular V1a receptors on vascular smooth muscle to cause vasoconstriction, elevating systemic blood pressure.
examTip: ADH (Vasopressin) dual actions: V1 receptors = Vasoconstriction (↑ TPR); V2 receptors = Water retention (↑ Blood Volume). Both elevate BP.

evidence.quote: A patient with an increased secretion of ADH. Which of the following ABP readings would be most likely? D. 165/100 mmHg

concept: Hypervolemia Trigger for Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP)
stem: An acute increase in total circulating blood volume and atrial distension stimulates the release of which of the following counter-regulatory hormones?

choices.rationale: Atrial myocytes release Atrial Natriuretic Peptide (ANP) in response to atrial stretch caused by hypervolemia, promoting natriuresis and vasodilation to lower blood volume.
ADH secretion is suppressed by hypervolemia via low-pressure cardiopulmonary stretch receptors.
Aldosterone secretion is suppressed when volume expands.
Hypervolemia suppresses renin and reduces Angiotensin II formation.

explanation: When blood volume expands, increased venous return stretches the atrial walls. Granules in atrial cardiomyocytes release ANP, which travels to kidneys and vasculature to promote sodium excretion (natriuresis), diuresis, and vasodilation, countering volume overload.
examTip: Atrial Stretch (Volume Overload) → Releases ANP (Atrial Natriuretic Peptide). ANP is the natural antagonist of RAAS and ADH.

evidence.quote: Increase in blood volume stimulates release of which of the following hormone? A. Atrial natriuretic peptide

concept: Atrial Natriuretic Peptide Physiological Actions and Renin Inhibition
stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) exerts all of the following physiological effects EXCEPT

choices.rationale: ANP relaxes vascular smooth muscle via cGMP, causing systemic arteriolar vasodilation.

choices.text: Increased excretion of Na+ and water
choices.rationale: ANP directly causes natriuresis and diuresis at the medullary collecting duct.
This is FALSE (the correct answer for EXCEPT): ANP INHIBITS renin secretion, inhibits aldosterone release, and inhibits ADH secretion to promote fluid loss.
By inducing sodium and water loss, ANP successfully reduces total circulating blood volume.

explanation: ANP acts via membrane-bound guanylyl cyclase-A receptors to increase cyclic GMP. It dilates afferent arterioles and constricts efferent arterioles (↑ GFR), suppresses sodium reabsorption in collecting ducts, and directly suppresses renin release by juxtaglomerular cells.
examTip: ANP actions: ↑ Natriuresis, ↑ Diuresis, Vasodilation, ↓ Renin, ↓ Aldosterone, ↓ ADH → Lowers blood volume and BP.

evidence.quote: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) causes all the following EXCEPT C. Stimulation of renin secretion
